217.summary: Decide whether an integer array contains any value more than once.
217.approach: Scan from left to right while storing values already seen in a set. A value already in the set proves a duplicate; reaching the end proves all values are distinct.
edgeCases: [7] → false
[4,4] → true
217.complexity: Expected O(n) time and O(n) space with hash-set operations.

242.summary: Check whether two strings have exactly the same characters with the same multiplicities.
242.approach: Reject different lengths, then compare character frequency counts. Matching counts are sufficient because the order of the characters does not affect an anagram.
edgeCases: "a", "a" → true
"aab", "abb" → false
"ab", "a" → false
242.complexity: O(n) time; O(1) space for the fixed lowercase alphabet, or O(u) for u distinct characters.

1.summary: Find two distinct array positions whose values add to a given target.
1.approach: Keep a map from each previously visited value to its index. Look up the current value’s complement before inserting the current index, which prevents using one position twice.
edgeCases: [3,3], target 6 → indices 0 and 1
[-3,4,3], target 0 → indices 0 and 2
[0,4,0], target 0 → indices 0 and 2
1.complexity: Expected O(n) time and O(n) space; the problem guarantees one answer.

49.summary: Collect strings into groups whose members are anagrams of one another.
49.approach: Give each word a canonical key made from its character counts, then append it to that key’s group. For lowercase English letters, a fixed 26-count signature avoids sorting each word.
edgeCases: ["", ""] → one two-item group
["ab", "ba", "aa"] → two groups
["a"] → one singleton group
49.complexity: O(total characters + number of words) time for a fixed alphabet; O(number of words) grouping references plus output and keys.

347.summary: Return the k distinct values that occur most frequently in an array.
347.approach: Count each value, then place it in a bucket indexed by its frequency. Read buckets from highest frequency downward until k values have been collected; the stated unique-answer condition resolves the cutoff.
edgeCases: [2,2,1], k=2 → both values
347.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space with frequency buckets; answer order is unrestricted.

238.summary: For every array position, compute the product of all values at other positions without division.
238.approach: Write the product strictly to the left of each position into the output. Sweep backward with a running suffix product and multiply it into each stored prefix, so zeros need no special division case.
238.complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space excluding the O(n) output. Respect the problem’s product bounds.

36.summary: Check whether the filled cells of a partially completed Sudoku board violate any row, column, or 3×3-box rule.
36.approach: Maintain separate seen-digit sets for each row, column, and box, ignoring empty cells. Reject a digit already present in any of its three sets; a valid partial board need not be solvable.
edgeCases: Two 5s in one row → false
Two equal digits only in the same 3×3 box → false
A board containing only dots → true
36.complexity: O(1) time and space for the fixed 9×9 board: only 81 cells are inspected.

271.summary: Design a reversible encoding that packs a list of strings into one string and recovers the exact original list.
271.approach: Prefix each string with its length and a separator, then concatenate the payloads. During decoding, parse a length first and consume exactly that many characters, so separators inside the payload remain ordinary data.
edgeCases: [] must remain distinct from [""]
["a#b", "12"] must round-trip
["", "", "x"] preserves all empty items
271.complexity: O(L) time and space for L encoded characters. Encoder and decoder must agree on character-versus-byte length, especially across languages.

128.summary: Find the length of the longest run of consecutive integer values, regardless of their positions in the array.
128.approach: Put values in a set and start counting only at a value whose predecessor is absent. Every distinct value then belongs to one forward scan, so duplicate values and overlapping starts do not multiply the work.
128.complexity: Expected O(n) time and O(n) space with a hash set; no sorting is required.

125.summary: Determine whether text reads the same forward and backward after ignoring non-alphanumeric characters and letter case.
125.approach: Compare characters from both ends, skipping punctuation and normalizing case before each comparison. An alternative is to build a normalized string and compare it with its reverse.
edgeCases: "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" → true
"., " → true
"0P" → false
125.complexity: Two pointers: O(n) time and O(1) space. A filtered-string implementation uses O(n) space; repeated immutable concatenation may add overhead.

167.summary: Find two entries in an ascending sorted array that sum to the target, returning their one-based positions.
167.approach: Place pointers at the two ends and inspect their sum. Move the left pointer when the sum is too small or the right pointer when it is too large; sorted order proves the discarded choices cannot work.
167.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space; one solution is guaranteed.

15.summary: Return each distinct triple of values that can be chosen from different array positions to sum to zero.
15.approach: Sort the array, fix one value, and use two pointers to find complementary pairs in the suffix. Skip repeated fixed values and repeated pair values so each value triple is emitted only once.
edgeCases: [1,2,3] → no triples
15.complexity: O(n²) time; O(1) scan space plus sorting workspace and O(r) output for r triples.

11.summary: Choose two vertical lines that enclose the greatest rectangular water area with the horizontal axis.
11.approach: Begin with the widest pair and track its area using the shorter line as the height. Move the shorter endpoint inward, since keeping it while reducing the width cannot improve that pair’s area.

42.summary: Calculate how much water remains between unit-width elevation bars after rainfall.
42.approach: Maintain the highest boundary seen from each end and advance the side with the lower boundary. That side’s water level is already determined by its own maximum, because the opposite side provides a boundary at least as high.
42.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space with two pointers.

121.summary: Find the greatest nonnegative profit from at most one buy followed by a later sell.
121.approach: Track the lowest price seen so far and evaluate the profit from selling on each day. Keep the answer at least zero so a falling market correctly favors making no trade.

3.summary: Find the length of the longest contiguous part of a string containing no repeated character.
3.approach: Maintain a window with a set or last-seen positions for its characters. When the next character repeats inside the window, advance the left boundary until uniqueness is restored before measuring the window.
edgeCases: "aaaa" → 1
"abba" → 2
3.complexity: O(n) time and O(min(n, alphabet size)) space. State whether character positions mean code points or UTF-16 units.

424.summary: Find the longest substring that can become one repeated uppercase letter after changing at most k characters.
424.approach: Keep window character counts and the highest frequency seen while expanding. A window needs its length minus its dominant frequency replacements; the historical maximum-frequency optimization preserves the best attainable length even when the retained window is temporarily not a fresh witness.
edgeCases: "AAAA", k=0 → 4
"ABAB", k=2 → 4
"AABABBA", k=1 → 4
424.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space for 26 uppercase letters using the historical-frequency technique.

567.summary: Check whether a string contains a contiguous rearrangement of every character in another string.
567.approach: Slide a window whose length equals the shorter pattern and compare its frequency counts with the pattern’s counts. Update only the entering and leaving letters, optionally maintaining the number of matching alphabet buckets.
edgeCases: "ab" in "eidbaooo" → true
"aab" in "ab" → false
"aab" in "baa" → true
567.complexity: O(m+n) time and O(1) space for the lowercase English alphabet.

76.summary: Find the shortest substring that includes every required character with its required multiplicity.
76.approach: Expand a sliding window until every required frequency is satisfied. Then repeatedly shrink from the left, recording the best window, until removing a character breaks coverage.
edgeCases: s="aa", t="aa" → "aa"
s="ADOBECODEBANC", t="ABC" → "BANC"
76.complexity: O(|s|+|t|) time and O(u) count storage, plus the returned substring; t is nonempty in the problem.

239.summary: Return the maximum value in every consecutive array window of size k.
239.approach: Keep candidate indices in a deque whose values decrease from front to back. Remove expired indices from the front and dominated values from the back; the front is always the current maximum.
239.complexity: O(n) time and O(k) deque space plus output. Use a real deque or head index, not repeated linear-cost Array.shift.

20.summary: Check whether a string of brackets closes every opening bracket in the correct nested order.
20.approach: Push opening brackets onto a stack. Each closing bracket must match and remove the most recent opener, and the stack must be empty at the end.
edgeCases: "([)]" → false
"(" → false
20.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) worst-case space.

155.summary: Implement a stack that also reports its smallest current value in constant time.
155.approach: Store the minimum-so-far alongside each pushed value, either in a parallel stack or in each stack entry. Pop the value and its recorded minimum together so duplicate minima and earlier minima are restored correctly.
edgeCases: Push 2,1,1; pop once → minimum 1
Push -2,0,-3; pop → minimum -2
One value serves as both top and minimum
155.complexity: O(1) per query and amortized O(1) array push/pop; O(n) storage. Nonempty-stack calls are guaranteed by the problem.

150.summary: Evaluate an arithmetic expression written with each operator after its two operands.
150.approach: Push numbers onto a stack and replace the top two operands with each operator’s result. Preserve operand order for subtraction and division, and truncate division toward zero rather than toward negative infinity.
150.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space for n tokens; inputs form a valid expression with no division by zero.

22.summary: Generate every properly nested string formed from n pairs of parentheses.
22.approach: Backtrack with counts of used opening and closing parentheses. Add an opener only while fewer than n have been used, and add a closer only while it cannot outnumber the openers in the prefix.
edgeCases: n=3 has 5 results with no duplicates
22.complexity: O(n·Cₙ) output time and space for Catalan number Cₙ; O(n) auxiliary recursion/path space.

739.summary: For each day, find how many days must pass before a strictly warmer temperature, or zero if none follows.
739.approach: Keep indices of unresolved days in a decreasing-temperature stack. A warmer day resolves and pops all cooler days on top; equal temperatures remain unresolved.
739.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space because each index is pushed and popped at most once.

853.summary: Count how many groups of cars reach a common target when cars cannot pass and a catching car joins the slower group ahead.
853.approach: Sort cars from closest to farthest from the target and compute each car’s unobstructed arrival time. A car whose time does not exceed the fleet ahead merges into it; a larger time starts a new fleet.
edgeCases: One car → one fleet
Two cars meeting exactly at the target → one fleet
target 10, positions [8,0], speeds [1,1] → two fleets
853.complexity: O(n log n) sorting time; O(n) sorted storage, with O(1) fleet-tracking state possible.

84.summary: Find the largest rectangle that fits entirely beneath adjacent histogram bars.
84.approach: Maintain increasing heights together with the earliest position where each height could start. When a lower bar arrives, pop taller bars and finalize their rectangles, carrying their starting position into the new bar.
84.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) stack space; flush remaining bars at the end.

704.summary: Locate a target in a strictly increasing integer array, returning its index or -1.
704.approach: Keep an inclusive interval that could still contain the target and compare its midpoint. Discard the midpoint and the impossible half on every unsuccessful comparison so the interval strictly shrinks.
edgeCases: [5], target 5 → 0
[5], target 4 → -1
704.complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) space.

74.summary: Test whether a target appears in a matrix whose rows are sorted and whose rows form one globally sorted sequence.
74.approach: Binary-search the row whose first and last values could contain the target, then binary-search within it. Equivalently, binary-search flattened indices and map each index back to a row and column.
edgeCases: [[1]], target 1 → true
[[1,3],[5,7]], target 4 → false
One-column matrix with target in the final row
74.complexity: O(log(rows·columns)) time and O(1) space; the cross-row ordering condition is essential.

875.summary: Find the slowest integer eating speed that finishes all banana piles within a fixed number of hours.
875.approach: For a candidate speed, add the ceiling of each pile size divided by that speed. Feasibility is monotone, so binary-search the first feasible speed between one and the largest pile.
edgeCases: h equals number of piles → speed is largest pile
One huge pile and many available hours
875.complexity: O(n log M) time and O(1) space, where M is the largest pile. Use exact ceiling arithmetic and a sufficiently wide hour sum.

153.summary: Find the smallest value in a rotated ascending array whose values are all distinct.
153.approach: Compare the midpoint with the right endpoint to determine which side contains the rotation minimum. Keep the midpoint when it could be the minimum and continue until one candidate remains.
153.complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) space; distinct values make the half-selection unambiguous.

33.summary: Find a target’s index in a rotated sorted array with distinct values, or return -1.
33.approach: At each midpoint, identify which half is still sorted. Check whether the target lies within that half’s value range and keep only the half that can contain it.
edgeCases: [1], target 0 → -1
Unrotated [1,2,3], target 3 → 2
33.complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) space under the no-duplicates constraint.

981.summary: Store timestamped values by key and retrieve the latest value whose timestamp does not exceed a query time.
981.approach: Append each write to its key’s timestamp-ordered history, using the problem’s increasing-write-time guarantee. Binary-search for the rightmost timestamp at most the query, returning an empty string when no such entry exists.
edgeCases: A missing key returns ""
Query before a key’s first write returns ""
Query exactly at a write returns that value
981.complexity: Amortized O(1) set; O(log m) get for m versions of the key; O(total writes) storage.

4.summary: Find the median of two sorted arrays without merging all of their elements.
4.approach: Binary-search a partition of the shorter array and derive the complementary partition in the other array. Once both left boundary values are no larger than the opposite right values, take the appropriate middle boundary or average the two middle boundaries.
4.complexity: O(log(min(m,n)+1)) time and O(1) space; at least one array is nonempty.

206.summary: Reverse the direction of a singly linked list and return its new head.
206.approach: Walk through the list with previous and current pointers, saving the next node before changing the current link. After each step, the processed prefix is reversed and the saved remainder is still reachable.
edgeCases: Empty list → empty list
One node remains unchanged
1→2→3 becomes 3→2→1
206.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space for the iterative approach.

21.summary: Combine two sorted linked lists into one sorted linked list.
21.approach: Use a dummy head and repeatedly attach the smaller current node from the two lists. Once one input is exhausted, attach the other remainder directly.
edgeCases: Two empty lists → empty list
An empty list plus 1→2 returns 1→2
1→1 and 1 merge into three nodes
21.complexity: O(m+n) time and O(1) auxiliary space when relinking iteratively; recursive merging adds O(m+n) stack space.

143.summary: Rearrange a linked list by alternately taking nodes from its beginning and end, without changing their values.
143.approach: Find the midpoint with slow and fast pointers, split the list, and reverse the second half. Weave the two halves together while preserving each next pointer before relinking.
edgeCases: One node stays unchanged
143.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space; explicitly split the halves to avoid a cycle.

19.summary: Remove the nth node counted backward from a linked list’s tail and return the resulting head.
19.approach: Start a trailing pointer at a dummy node and advance a leading pointer n nodes from the head. Move both until the leader reaches the end, leaving the trailer immediately before the node to remove.
edgeCases: One node, n=1 → empty list
19.complexity: O(length) time and O(1) space; n is guaranteed to name an existing node.

138.summary: Deep-copy a linked list whose nodes have both next and arbitrary random pointers.
138.approach: Create one fresh node for every original node and store an original-to-copy map. In a second pass, translate both pointers through that map so aliases, cycles through random links, and null links are preserved without referencing originals.
edgeCases: A node whose random pointer targets itself
Several nodes sharing one random target
Empty list → empty copy
138.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) mapping space plus O(n) copied nodes; interleaving nodes is an optional O(1)-auxiliary alternative.

2.summary: Add two nonnegative integers represented by linked lists of decimal digits in least-significant-first order.
2.approach: Advance through both lists while carrying the tens part of each digit sum. Continue until both lists and the carry are exhausted, emitting each remainder digit into a new list.
edgeCases: 0 plus 0 → one zero node
Unequal list lengths preserve the longer remainder
2.complexity: O(max(m,n)) time and output space; O(1) working state, without converting whole numbers to machine integers.

141.summary: Determine whether following next pointers in a linked list eventually revisits a node.
141.approach: Advance one pointer by one link and another by two links. They must eventually meet inside a cycle, while reaching a null pointer proves the list ends.
edgeCases: Empty list → false
One node pointing to itself → true
Equal-valued separate nodes without a back-link → false
141.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space; compare node identity, not node values.

287.summary: Find the repeated value in an array of n+1 values drawn from 1 through n, without modifying the array.
287.approach: Treat each array value as the next index in a functional graph. Floyd’s cycle detection finds a meeting point, then resetting one pointer to index zero and advancing both one step identifies the cycle entrance, which is the duplicate value.
287.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space; depends on the stated index range and exactly one repeated value.

146.summary: Build a fixed-capacity key-value cache that evicts the least recently used entry and updates recency on reads and writes.
146.approach: Map keys to nodes in a doubly linked recency list. Move accessed or updated nodes to the most-recent end and remove the least-recent node when inserting beyond capacity.
edgeCases: Capacity 1 evicts the old key on a new insert
Updating a key changes its value and recency
A failed get returns -1 without adding an entry
146.complexity: Expected O(1) get/put and O(capacity) storage with a hash map and linked list.

23.summary: Merge several sorted linked lists into one sorted linked list.
23.approach: Merge lists in pairs, then repeat on the smaller collection until one list remains. This balanced merge schedule makes each node participate in only logarithmically many merges; a heap of current list heads is another option.
edgeCases: No lists → empty result
A mixture of empty and nonempty lists
All lists contain repeated equal values
23.complexity: O(N log(k+1)) time for N total nodes and k lists; O(k) head-array workspace for pairwise merging, reusing existing nodes.

25.summary: Reverse each complete block of k nodes in a linked list, leaving a shorter final block in its original order.
25.approach: Before changing links, find the kth node to confirm the whole block exists. Reverse the block toward the following node, reconnect its new head, and use its old head as the predecessor for the next block.
edgeCases: k=1 leaves the list unchanged
Five nodes with k=2 leave the last node unchanged
k equal to list length reverses the entire list
25.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space; values remain unchanged and only links are rewired.

226.summary: Mirror a binary tree by swapping the left and right children of every node.
226.approach: Swap the two children at the current node and repeat for each subtree. Null children form the base case, and the returned root is the same node with mirrored descendants.
edgeCases: Empty tree stays empty
A leaf stays unchanged
A left-only chain becomes a right-only chain
226.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space, with height h reaching n for a chain.

104.summary: Return the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path in a binary tree.
104.approach: Compute one plus the larger depth of the two child subtrees, with a null subtree contributing zero. An explicit stack or level-order traversal can replace recursion when the tree is very deep.
edgeCases: Empty tree → 0
Single node → 1
A chain of four nodes → 4
104.complexity: O(n) time; O(h) DFS space or O(w) BFS space for maximum level width w.

543.summary: Find the largest number of edges on any simple path between two nodes in a binary tree.
543.approach: During a postorder traversal, return each subtree’s height. At every node, the sum of its two child heights is a candidate diameter through that node, even when the best path never reaches the root.
edgeCases: Single node → diameter 0
A four-node chain → diameter 3
The longest path may lie wholly inside one subtree
543.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space; diameter counts edges, while returned heights count nodes.

110.summary: Check whether every node’s left and right subtree heights differ by at most one.
110.approach: Return both height and balance status from a postorder traversal, or use a failure sentinel. A node is balanced only when both descendants are balanced and their heights differ by no more than one.
edgeCases: Empty tree → true
Single node → true
A three-node one-sided chain → false
110.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space; avoid separately recomputing heights at each node.

100.summary: Check whether two binary trees have the same shape and the same values at corresponding nodes.
100.approach: Compare paired nodes together: two nulls match, but one null or unequal values fail. Recursively require both left pairs and both right pairs to match.
edgeCases: Two empty trees → true
Equal values with different left/right placement → false
One differing leaf value → false
100.complexity: O(min(n,m)) inspected nodes before termination, O(n) when both size-n trees match; O(h) recursion space.

572.summary: Determine whether one binary tree appears as an entire rooted subtree inside another tree.
572.approach: At each candidate root in the larger tree, compare both trees for exact shape and value equality. If they do not match there, search the candidate’s left and right descendants.
edgeCases: Identical trees → true
Matching values but an extra child in the candidate → false
A matching leaf anywhere in the larger tree → true
572.complexity: O(nm) worst-case time for tree sizes n and m; O(h₁+h₂) recursion space. Serialization with linear pattern matching can improve the time bound.

235.summary: Find the lowest ancestor shared by two existing nodes in a binary search tree with distinct values.
235.approach: Use the BST ordering to descend while both target values lie strictly on the same side of the current node. The first split, or the first target encountered, is their lowest common ancestor.
edgeCases: Targets on opposite sides → current root
One target is an ancestor of the other → that target
Both targets deep in the same subtree
235.complexity: O(h) time and O(1) space iteratively; O(n) time in a skewed BST.

102.summary: Return a binary tree’s values grouped by depth, from left to right within each level.
102.approach: Use a queue and capture its length before processing a level. Remove exactly that many nodes, record their values, and append their children for the next level.
edgeCases: Empty tree → []
Single node → one one-item level
A missing left child does not create a placeholder
102.complexity: O(n) time, O(w) live queue space, and O(n) output. JavaScript needs a deque or head index to preserve the time bound.

199.summary: Return the visible node value at each depth when looking at a binary tree from its right side.
199.approach: Traverse the tree level by level and keep the last real node seen in each level. A right-first depth-first search also works if it records only the first node encountered at each depth.
edgeCases: Empty tree → []
A left-only chain is fully visible
A deeper left subtree can appear below a shallow right subtree
199.complexity: O(n) time; O(w) BFS space or O(h) right-first DFS space, plus O(h) output.

1448.summary: Count nodes whose value is at least every value on the path from the root to that node.
1448.approach: Carry the maximum value encountered on the current root-to-node path during a traversal. Count the node when it reaches or exceeds that maximum, then pass the updated maximum separately into each child.
edgeCases: The root is always counted
Equal-valued ancestors do not disqualify a node
All-negative node values require a negative initial maximum
1448.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) traversal space.

98.summary: Determine whether a binary tree satisfies strict binary-search-tree ordering throughout every subtree.
98.approach: Pass an exclusive lower and upper bound into each recursive call. Each node must lie between both bounds, and its value tightens the bound for its left or right descendants.
edgeCases: Equal parent and child values → false
A deep left descendant larger than the root → false
A valid one-node tree → true
98.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space. This problem rejects duplicates, unlike some other BST conventions.

230.summary: Find the kth smallest value in a binary search tree, with k counted from one.
230.approach: Perform an in-order traversal, which visits BST values in ascending order. Stop after the kth visited node rather than traversing the whole tree unnecessarily.
edgeCases: k=1 returns the minimum
k equals node count returns the maximum
A skewed tree still needs ancestor stack space
230.complexity: O(h+k) time and O(h) stack space; O(n) in the worst case. Repeated rank queries can use maintained subtree sizes.

105.summary: Rebuild a binary tree from its preorder and inorder traversals when all values are distinct.
105.approach: The next preorder value is the current subtree’s root, and its inorder position divides the left and right subtrees. Use an inorder-index map and index ranges to recurse without repeatedly searching or copying array slices.
edgeCases: One value creates one leaf
A preorder/inorder pair describing a one-sided chain
A root with no left subtree uses an empty left range
105.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) map plus O(h) stack using an index map and ranges; repeated searches and slices can make reconstruction quadratic.

124.summary: Find the greatest sum along any nonempty simple path in a binary tree, allowing the path to start and end anywhere.
124.approach: Each recursive call returns the best one-branch contribution it can give its parent. Separately update a global answer with the node plus both nonnegative child contributions, since a completed path may bend at this node.
edgeCases: All values negative → the least-negative node
A single negative node cannot be replaced by an empty path
The best path can exclude the root
124.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space.

297.summary: Design a serialization format that reconstructs a binary tree’s values and exact shape.
297.approach: Write a preorder stream containing both node values and explicit null markers. Decode by consuming one token at a time and recursively constructing exactly two children for each non-null token.
edgeCases: Empty tree needs an unambiguous representation
Left-only and right-only trees must encode differently
Negative and multi-digit values must round-trip
297.complexity: O(n) tokens and O(h) stack with an advancing cursor; serialized size also includes digit lengths. Repeatedly removing the first token from an array can make decoding O(n²).

208.summary: Implement insertion, full-word lookup, and prefix lookup for a collection of lowercase words.
208.approach: Store one character per trie edge so words share common prefixes. Mark complete-word endpoints separately, because reaching the end of a prefix does not prove that the prefix itself was inserted as a word.
edgeCases: Insert "apple"; search "app" is false
Insert "app" later; both words remain present
Repeated insertion does not duplicate trie paths
208.complexity: O(L) per operation for length L; O(total inserted characters) worst-case nodes for a fixed alphabet.

211.summary: Maintain a word collection that supports searches where a dot matches any single letter.
211.approach: Insert words into a trie with explicit end-of-word markers. Follow one edge for an ordinary letter, but recursively try each existing child for a dot, requiring the entire pattern to end at a complete word.
edgeCases: Pattern "." matches only one-letter words
"b.." can match "bad"
A prefix without a word endpoint does not match
211.complexity: Insert O(L); search visits matching trie branches, up to O(a^L) in the all-wildcard worst case, bounded by stored trie nodes; O(L) search stack.

212.summary: Find dictionary words that can be traced through adjacent board cells without reusing a cell within one word.
212.approach: Build a trie for the dictionary and backtrack from each cell while following only existing trie edges. Mark the current path’s cells as used, restore them on return, and suppress already-reported word endpoints; removing exhausted prefixes adds pruning.
edgeCases: A dictionary word may be a prefix of another
One word reachable by several paths is reported once
A word requiring a cell to be revisited is rejected
212.complexity: Loose worst-case O(S + RC·4^L·L) with copied path strings, where S is dictionary length and L maximum word length; trie pruning helps. O(S+RC+L) working space plus output.

703.summary: Maintain the kth largest value as new numbers are added to a stream, counting duplicate values separately.
703.approach: Keep a min heap containing only the largest k values encountered so far. Insert each new value and discard the minimum when the heap grows past k; the retained minimum is the kth largest.
edgeCases: k=1 tracks the running maximum
Duplicate values occupy separate ranks
The initial collection may have fewer than k elements
703.complexity: O(log k) per add and O(k) retained storage; a size-k construction costs O(n log k) for n initial values.

1046.summary: Repeatedly smash the two heaviest stones, replacing unequal weights by their difference, and report the final weight or zero.
1046.approach: Store weights in a max heap so the next pair of heaviest stones is always available. Remove two weights each round and reinsert their positive difference; equal weights vanish together.
1046.complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) heap space; a min heap can emulate a max heap with negated weights.

973.summary: Select k points having the smallest Euclidean distances from the origin.
973.approach: Compare squared distances to avoid square roots. A heap of all points can expose the nearest k, while a size-k max heap keeps only the best candidates as points arrive.
edgeCases: A point at [0,0] has distance zero
Equal distances allow any valid boundary choice
k equals the number of points
973.complexity: All-points min-heap approach: O(n+k log n) time, O(n) space; size-k alternative: O(n log k) time, O(k) auxiliary space.

215.summary: Return the kth largest array value, counting repeated values as separate ranks.
215.approach: Use a min heap of the largest k values, or partition around a pivot and recurse only into the partition containing the desired rank. Quickselect avoids fully sorting the array, but its guarantees depend on pivot selection and partition implementation.
edgeCases: k=1 returns the maximum
k=n returns the minimum
215.complexity: Size-k heap: O(n log k) time/O(k) space. Randomized in-place quickselect: expected O(n), worst O(n²); out-of-place partition variants allocate extra arrays.

621.summary: Schedule unit-time tasks with at least n intervening time slots between equal task types, minimizing total time including idle slots.
621.approach: The most frequent task creates the minimum number of separated frames, and equally frequent task types fill the final frame. Compare that frame bound with the total task count, because plentiful other tasks can fill every idle slot.
edgeCases: Cooldown n=0 → number of tasks
[A,A,A], n=2 → 7 slots
[A,A,B,B], n=1 → 4 slots
621.complexity: O(T+a) time and O(a) frequency space for T tasks and a types; a=26 in the problem. Heap simulation is an alternative.

355.summary: Implement posting, following, unfollowing, and a feed containing the ten newest tweets from a user and their followees.
355.approach: Keep each user’s posts in timestamp order and store follow relationships in sets. Seed a heap with each relevant user’s newest post, then merge backward through those histories until ten tweets have been emitted.
edgeCases: A user always sees their own posts
Following the same user twice must not duplicate tweets
Unfollowing removes that user’s posts from later feeds
355.complexity: Expected O(1) posting/follow updates; feed O(F log F + 10 log F) with individual heap insertions for F relevant users; O(posts+follow edges) persistent storage.

295.summary: Support inserting numbers and querying the median of all values seen so far.
295.approach: Keep the lower half in a max heap and the upper half in a min heap. Preserve cross-heap ordering and rebalance sizes to differ by at most one, so one root or the average of two roots determines the median.
edgeCases: One inserted value is its own median
Repeated equal values must remain separate observations
295.complexity: O(log n) insertion, O(1) median query, and O(n) space; median queries occur only after an insertion.

78.summary: Generate every subset of an array whose values are distinct.
78.approach: Backtrack through the array, deciding for each position whether to include it. Copy the current subset at each completed decision path so later mutations do not change earlier results.
edgeCases: A singleton produces [] and its singleton subset
The empty subset must appear
n distinct values produce exactly 2^n subsets
78.complexity: O(n·2^n) time and output space; O(n) auxiliary recursion/path space.

39.summary: List all unique combinations of positive candidate values that sum to a target, allowing each value to be reused.
39.approach: Backtrack in nondecreasing candidate-index order to avoid producing different permutations of the same combination. Taking a candidate keeps its index available; skipping it moves forward, and a sum above the target ends the branch.
edgeCases: [2], target 1 → no combinations
39.complexity: Output-sensitive exponential time; a loose bound is O(C^(T/minCandidate)·T/minCandidate). O(T/minCandidate) path space plus output for C candidates and target T.

46.summary: Generate every ordering of an array of distinct values.
46.approach: Choose an unused value for each next position and undo that choice when returning from recursion. Emit a copy only after all positions are filled, ensuring every sequence corresponds to one complete set of choices.
edgeCases: Two distinct values produce two orderings
Three distinct values produce six orderings
46.complexity: O(n·n!) time and output space; O(n) working space with an in-place or used-array backtracker. Rotating/slicing implementations add allocation overhead.

90.summary: Generate all distinct subsets of an array that may contain duplicate values.
90.approach: Sort the values so equal candidates are adjacent. At each decision depth, skip repeated alternative choices, while still allowing multiple copies of a value when they come from distinct positions in the same chosen subset.
edgeCases: [1,2,2] has six distinct subsets
The empty subset appears exactly once
90.complexity: O(n log n + n·2^n) worst-case time; O(n) working space plus output, which can contain 2^n subsets.

40.summary: Find unique combinations summing to a target when each candidate occurrence may be used at most once.
40.approach: Sort the candidates and backtrack from a moving start index. Advance past a chosen position for the next call and skip equal alternatives at the same depth so duplicate input values do not create duplicate combinations.
edgeCases: [1,1], target 1 → one [1] result
[2,5], target 4 → no result
40.complexity: O(n log n + n·2^n) worst-case time; O(n) working space plus output. Positive values enable target-based pruning.

79.summary: Check whether a word can be spelled by moving horizontally or vertically through a board without reusing a cell.
79.approach: Try each matching starting cell and backtrack through neighbors that match the next letter. Mark cells only for the current path and restore them afterward, since a failed start must not block later starts.
edgeCases: One matching cell spells a one-letter word
Diagonal adjacency alone cannot form a word
"ABA" on two cells A,B fails because reuse is forbidden
79.complexity: O(RC·4^L) simple worst-case time, tightened to O(RC·3^L) after the first move; O(min(L,RC)) path/stack space.

131.summary: List every way to split a string into contiguous pieces that are each palindromes.
131.approach: From the current start index, try each endpoint whose substring is a palindrome and recurse on the remaining suffix. Record the current list of pieces when the entire string has been consumed; a precomputed palindrome table avoids repeated checks.
edgeCases: "aaa" has four valid partitions
131.complexity: Exponential output, up to O(n·2^n) output characters. Palindrome-table preprocessing costs O(n²); repeated scans and slicing can add overhead.

17.summary: Generate every letter string represented by a sequence of telephone keypad digits from 2 through 9.
17.approach: Backtrack one digit at a time and choose each letter assigned to that digit. Emit a string only when every digit has contributed one letter; an empty digit string produces no combinations.
edgeCases: Empty digits → []
Digit 7 has four choices
Digits 23 produce nine two-letter strings
17.complexity: O(L·4^L) worst-case time/output and O(L) working recursion space for L digits.

51.summary: Place n queens on an n×n chessboard so none share a row, column, or diagonal, returning every valid board.
51.approach: Place one queen per row and track occupied columns and the two diagonal identifiers row+column and row-column. Undo all three markings when backtracking, and copy the board only after all rows are placed.
edgeCases: n=1 has one board
n=2 and n=3 have no solutions
n=4 has two boards
51.complexity: Exponential search; a safe O(n·n! + S·n²) bound includes scanning columns and copying S boards. O(n²) board plus O(n) search state, excluding output.

200.summary: Count groups of land cells connected horizontally or vertically in a binary grid.
200.approach: Scan for unvisited land and start one flood fill for each new component. Mark land as soon as it is discovered so the same component is never counted twice.
edgeCases: All water → 0
Two diagonal land cells count as two islands
One solid land rectangle → 1
200.complexity: O(RC) time and O(RC) worst-case queue/stack or visited storage. Mutating the grid removes a visited set, not the recursion-space cost.

133.summary: Deep-copy the connected component reachable from a node in an undirected graph.
133.approach: Map each original node to exactly one new node and create that mapping before exploring neighbors. Reuse mapped copies when an edge returns to an already-seen node, preserving cycles and shared neighbors.
edgeCases: Null starting node → null
One isolated node creates one isolated copy
A cycle must close among copied nodes only
133.complexity: O(V+E) time and O(V) mapping/traversal space plus O(V+E) copied output.

695.summary: Find the largest number of horizontally or vertically connected land cells in a binary grid.
695.approach: Flood-fill each unvisited land component and sum one for each cell reached. Compare each component’s size with the best area seen, while marking cells to prevent double counting.
edgeCases: All water → 0
One land cell → 1
Diagonal land cells remain separate components
695.complexity: O(RC) time and O(RC) worst-case traversal/visited space.

417.summary: Find cells from which downhill-or-level water can reach both the top/left borders and the bottom/right borders.
417.approach: Reverse the direction of reasoning and flood-fill inward from each ocean’s borders, allowing moves to equal or higher cells. The intersection of the two reachable sets gives cells with a valid downhill path to each ocean.
edgeCases: A single cell reaches both oceans
A flat grid lets every cell reach both
An enclosed low basin may reach neither ocean
417.complexity: O(RC) time and O(RC) space; each ocean visits each cell at most once.

130.summary: Change every O-region fully enclosed by X cells into X while preserving O-regions connected to a border.
130.approach: Flood-fill from border O cells and mark every O connected to them as safe. After that traversal, flip only unmarked O cells and restore any temporary safe markers.
edgeCases: A border O is never captured
An interior O linked to a border through a narrow corridor survives
A surrounded one-cell O flips to X
130.complexity: O(RC) time and O(RC) worst-case traversal space, even with in-place markers.

994.summary: Find how many minutes are needed for all fresh oranges to rot when rot spreads one cell per minute, or return -1 if some remain unreachable.
994.approach: Start a breadth-first search with every initially rotten orange already in the queue. Process one whole frontier per minute and decrement a fresh count when cells first become rotten, stopping once the count reaches zero.
edgeCases: No fresh oranges initially → 0
Fresh oranges with no rotten source → -1
An empty-cell barrier can leave fresh oranges unreachable
994.complexity: O(RC) time and O(RC) queue space; mark on enqueue so each cell enters once.

286.summary: Fill each empty room with its shortest walking distance to any gate, respecting walls and leaving unreachable rooms unchanged.
286.approach: Initialize a breadth-first queue with all gates at distance zero. Expand simultaneously into unvisited empty rooms, assigning distance on first arrival so the closest gate wins automatically.
edgeCases: No gates → all empty rooms stay at the infinity marker
Walls are never overwritten
An empty room beside two gates receives distance 1
286.complexity: O(RC) time and O(RC) queue/visited space; use the room’s assigned distance as a visited marker if desired.

207.summary: Determine whether all courses can be completed given prerequisite dependencies.
207.approach: Treat prerequisites as directed edges and detect a cycle with visiting and completed states. Encountering a node already on the active DFS path proves an impossible dependency loop; completed nodes can be skipped safely.
edgeCases: No prerequisites → true
A course depending on itself → false
A cycle in a disconnected component still makes the answer false
207.complexity: O(V+E) time and O(V+E) storage including adjacency; O(V) traversal state.

210.summary: Produce any course order that places every prerequisite before its dependent course, or return an empty list when impossible.
210.approach: Traverse prerequisites with separate active-path and completed states. Append each course only after its prerequisites are finished, and abandon the result if an active-path revisit reveals a cycle.
edgeCases: Independent courses may appear in any order
A cycle returns []
Disconnected prerequisite chains must all appear
210.complexity: O(V+E) time and O(V+E) space including graph, traversal, and output.

684.summary: Find the extra edge whose removal restores an undirected graph formed by adding one edge to a tree.
684.approach: Process edges in input order with disjoint-set union. An edge whose endpoints already share a representative closes the unique cycle; it is the last edge of that cycle encountered in input order.
edgeCases: Triangle edges return the edge that closes the triangle
The extra edge need not be the final input edge
Vertices may already be indirectly connected by several edges
684.complexity: O(E·α(V)) amortized time and O(V) space with path compression and union by size/rank.

323.summary: Count connected components in an undirected graph, including vertices with no edges.
323.approach: Start with one component per vertex and union the endpoints of each edge. Decrease the component count only when two different representatives merge, or count distinct representatives after all edges are processed.
edgeCases: n isolated vertices → n components
A connected cycle → one component
An edge inside an existing component must not decrement twice
323.complexity: With union by rank and path compression: O((V+E)·α(V)) time/O(V) space; DFS is O(V+E). Both union balancing and path compression are needed for the stated amortized DSU bound.

261.summary: Check whether an undirected graph on all supplied vertices is a single tree.
261.approach: Require both connectivity and absence of cycles. A traversal skips only the edge back to its parent, rejects other revisits, and finally checks that every vertex was reached.
edgeCases: One vertex and no edges → true
Two disconnected trees → false
A connected graph with one cycle → false
261.complexity: O(V+E) time and O(V+E) adjacency/traversal space; V≥1 in the usual problem contract.

127.summary: Find the shortest sequence of valid words transforming a start word into an end word by changing one letter at a time.
127.approach: Connect words through shared wildcard patterns and run BFS from the start word. Count words rather than edges in the returned sequence length, and clear a pattern bucket after expanding it to avoid repeatedly scanning the same neighbors.
edgeCases: End word absent from the dictionary → 0
A one-change transformation returns 2
A present end word can still be unreachable
127.complexity: Target O(N·L²) time and pattern-string storage when constructing length-L wildcard keys; clearing buckets avoids repeated scans. BFS state is O(N).

332.summary: Use every airline ticket exactly once to build the lexicographically smallest valid itinerary beginning at JFK.
332.approach: Treat tickets as directed multigraph edges and apply an Eulerian-path traversal, consuming destinations in lexical order. Append an airport only after its outgoing tickets are exhausted, then reverse the postorder result so early dead ends land in the correct final position.
edgeCases: Duplicate tickets must be consumed separately
A lexically smallest next airport can be an immediate dead end
The final itinerary has one more airport than tickets
332.complexity: O(E log E) time/O(E) space using sorted adjacency with end-pops; avoid repeated front-pops and list copies.

1584.summary: Connect all given points with minimum total Manhattan-distance edge cost.
1584.approach: Build a minimum spanning tree, repeatedly connecting the cheapest point outside the current tree. Prim’s algorithm can compute distances on demand, avoiding storage of every edge in the complete graph.
edgeCases: One point → cost 0
Two points → their Manhattan distance
The shortest tour is a different problem from this tree
1584.complexity: Dense Prim: O(n²) time/O(n) space. Materializing all edges and using a heap can cost O(n² log n) time and O(n²) space.

743.summary: Find the time when a signal sent from one node has reached every node in a directed weighted network, or report failure.
743.approach: Use Dijkstra’s algorithm from the source because edge travel times are nonnegative. The answer is the largest finalized shortest-path distance if all nodes are reached, otherwise -1.
edgeCases: An unreachable node forces -1
The source’s arrival time is zero
A later-discovered multi-edge path may beat a direct edge
743.complexity: O((V+E) log V) with a standard heap-based Dijkstra implementation; O(V+E) space, including lazy duplicate heap entries.

778.summary: Find the earliest water level at which a path connects the top-left and bottom-right cells of an elevation grid.
778.approach: A path’s cost is its highest elevation, not the sum of elevations. Use a priority queue to expand the currently cheapest maximum-elevation path, relaxing a neighbor with the maximum of the current cost and its height.
edgeCases: A single cell’s answer is its own elevation
The endpoint height is a lower bound on the answer
A longer low-elevation route can beat a short high route
778.complexity: O(N² log N) time and O(N²) space for an N×N grid.

269.summary: Infer an ordering of all characters from words already sorted according to an unknown alphabet.
269.approach: Compare adjacent words and add only the first differing character’s precedence edge. Reject a longer word placed before its exact prefix, then topologically sort all characters and reject directed cycles.
edgeCases: ["abc","ab"] is invalid
["z","x","z"] creates a cycle
Characters without ordering edges must still appear
269.complexity: O(S+A+E) time and O(A+E) space for S input characters, A distinct symbols, and E deduplicated precedence edges.

787.summary: Find the cheapest flight route using at most k intermediate stops, or return -1 if no such route exists.
787.approach: Perform k+1 rounds of edge relaxation, where each round reads only the previous round’s distance array. Copying the array prevents updates from chaining through too many flights within one round.
edgeCases: k=0 allows only a direct flight
The cheapest unlimited-stop route may be invalid
No valid route within the stop budget → -1
787.complexity: O((k+1)(V+E)) time for copied-array Bellman-Ford rounds and O(V) working space; k stops means at most k+1 edges.

70.summary: Count ways to climb n stairs when each move takes either one or two stairs.
70.approach: The last move comes from either one stair below or two stairs below, so their counts add. Keep just the previous two counts instead of storing the full dynamic-programming table.
70.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) working space under bounded integer arithmetic; larger generalized inputs may require BigInt.

746.summary: Find the least cost to reach just beyond a staircase, paying for each step used and moving one or two steps at a time.
746.approach: For each step, compute its own cost plus the cheaper cost-to-finish of the next two steps. The answer is the better result from starting at step zero or step one; rolling states can avoid mutating the input.
edgeCases: With two steps, choose the cheaper starting step
746.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space; a backward DP may overwrite the input, while rolling states preserve it.

198.summary: Choose nonadjacent houses on a street to maximize the total money collected.
198.approach: For each house, compare skipping it with taking its value plus the best result from two houses earlier. Keep only the previous two best totals because no older state is needed.
edgeCases: One house → its value

213.summary: Maximize money collected from nonadjacent houses arranged in a circle, where the first and last houses are neighbors.
213.approach: A valid selection must exclude either the first house or the last house. Solve those two ordinary linear-house ranges and take the larger result, handling a single house separately.
edgeCases: One house may be taken
213.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) working space with index ranges; copying subarray slices instead uses O(n) extra space.

5.summary: Return a longest contiguous substring that reads the same forward and backward.
5.approach: Expand around every possible odd-length and even-length center while the endpoint characters match. Track only the best start and length, then extract the winning substring once to avoid repeated copying.
edgeCases: "cbbd" → "bb"
"babad" permits "bab" or "aba"
5.complexity: O(n²) time and O(1) working space, plus output. Center expansion is the target here; Manacher’s algorithm can achieve O(n).

647.summary: Count all contiguous palindromic substrings, treating equal text at different positions as separate occurrences.
647.approach: Expand around every single-character center and every gap between adjacent characters. Each successful expansion identifies one new palindrome, and every palindrome has exactly one such center.
edgeCases: "aaa" → 6
"abc" → 3
647.complexity: O(n²) time and O(1) auxiliary space with center expansion.

91.summary: Count how many ways a digit string can be decoded when numbers 1 through 26 map to letters.
91.approach: At each index, combine the ways from taking a valid one-digit code and a valid two-digit code. A leading zero contributes no one-digit option, and only values 10 through 26 may form a two-digit option.
91.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) memo/table space, reducible to O(1) rolling state.

322.summary: Find the fewest coins needed to reach an exact amount with unlimited copies of the supplied denominations.
322.approach: Let the best count for zero be zero and initialize other amounts as unreachable. For each amount, try every coin as the final coin and improve from the smaller amount, returning -1 if the target remains unreachable.
edgeCases: Amount 0 → 0 coins
Coins [2], amount 3 → -1
Coins [1,3,4], amount 6 → 2
322.complexity: O(C·A) time and O(A) space for C denominations and amount A; this is pseudo-polynomial in A.

152.summary: Find the largest product of any nonempty contiguous subarray.
152.approach: Track both the largest and smallest products ending at the current position. A negative value can swap their roles, while choosing the current value alone naturally restarts the subarray after a zero or an unfavorable prefix.
152.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space; update both extrema from the previous state, not partially updated values.

139.summary: Decide whether a string can be fully divided into dictionary words, with dictionary entries reusable.
139.approach: Define whether each suffix can be segmented and work backward from the empty suffix. At an index, a dictionary word is useful only if it matches there and the suffix after it is already known to be segmentable.
edgeCases: "applepenapple" with apple,pen → true
A matching prefix with an impossible suffix → false
A dictionary word may be used multiple times
139.complexity: Dictionary-word-loop DP: O(n·Σ|word|) worst-case time from substring comparisons; O(n) DP space. A trie can reduce repeated matching work.

300.summary: Find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence, whose chosen elements need not be adjacent.
300.approach: A direct DP records the best subsequence starting at each position by testing later larger values. For an O(n log n) target, maintain the smallest possible tail for each subsequence length and binary-search the first tail not smaller than the new value.
300.complexity: Pairwise DP: O(n²) time/O(n) space. Binary-search tails: O(n log n) time/O(n) space; equal values replace rather than extend.

416.summary: Decide whether all positive array values can be split into two groups with equal sums.
416.approach: Reject an odd total and reduce the problem to reaching half of the total with a subset. Update reachable sums once per item using a new set or a descending DP scan, which prevents accidentally reusing an item.
edgeCases: Odd total → false
416.complexity: O(n·S) time and O(S) space for target S=total/2, using bounded sums; pseudo-polynomial rather than polynomial in the input bit length.

62.summary: Count paths from the top-left to the bottom-right of an empty rectangular grid using only right and down moves.
62.approach: Each cell’s path count is the sum of the neighboring counts in the two allowed continuation directions. Initialize the outer row or column to one and reuse a single row of DP values.
edgeCases: A 1×1 grid → 1
A single row or column → 1
A 3×2 grid → 3
62.complexity: O(rows·columns) time and O(min(rows,columns)) space when choosing the shorter dimension for the DP row.

1143.summary: Find the maximum number of characters that can appear in the same order in two strings, with gaps allowed.
1143.approach: Use a DP state for a pair of suffix starting positions. Equal characters may be taken together; otherwise choose the better result from skipping one character in either string.
edgeCases: "abc", "abc" → 3
"abc", "def" → 0
"abcde", "ace" → 3
1143.complexity: O(mn) time and O(mn) table space; length-only queries can use O(min(m,n)) rolling space.

309.summary: Maximize profit from repeated stock trades when selling forces a one-day pause before the next purchase.
309.approach: Track the day and whether the next action may buy or must sell. Compare acting with waiting, and after a sale jump two days before returning to a buying state so the cooldown is enforced.
edgeCases: Strictly decreasing prices → 0
309.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) memo/stack space; an iterative hold/sold/rest formulation reduces working space to O(1).

518.summary: Count unordered combinations of unlimited coins that add to an exact amount.
518.approach: Process denominations in a fixed order so different coin orders do not count separately. A state can either skip the current denomination or use it again, with amount zero contributing one empty combination.
edgeCases: Amount 0 → 1 combination
Coins [2], amount 3 → 0
Coins [1,2,5], amount 5 → 4
518.complexity: O(C·A) time; O(A) space with denomination-outer 1-D DP, or O(C·A) memo/table space.

494.summary: Count assignments of a plus or minus sign to every array position whose resulting sum equals the target.
494.approach: Memoize the number of ways from a state consisting of the current index and accumulated sum. Branch on both signs even for zero, because plus-zero and minus-zero represent different assignments.
edgeCases: [0], target 0 → 2
A target outside ±sum(values) → 0
494.complexity: O(n·(2S+1)) time and memo space for S=sum(values), plus O(n) recursion; reachable-state sparsity may reduce work.

97.summary: Check whether a third string can be formed by weaving two strings together while preserving the order within each.
97.approach: Reject a length mismatch first, then define a state by how many characters have been consumed from each source. The next character must match an available source character, and either valid continuation may lead to a solution.
edgeCases: Three empty strings → true
One empty source reduces to equality with the other
Repeated characters may require trying both source choices
97.complexity: O(mn) time and O(mn) space, reducible to O(min(m,n)) rolling space.

329.summary: Find the longest path through horizontally or vertically adjacent matrix cells whose values strictly increase.
329.approach: Memoize the best increasing path starting at each cell and extend only into larger neighbors. Strict increase prevents cycles, so a cell’s cached result depends only on its position, not on the path used to reach it.
edgeCases: One cell → 1
An all-equal matrix → 1
The best path may start in an interior cell
329.complexity: O(RC) time and O(RC) memo plus worst-case recursion space; each cell examines at most four neighbors.

115.summary: Count how many different choices of positions in a source string spell a target string in order.
115.approach: For each pair of source and target indices, always allow skipping the source character. When the characters match, also count taking it; an exhausted target contributes one completed choice, while an exhausted source with target remaining contributes zero.
edgeCases: "aaa" → "aa" has 3 choices
A target longer than the source has 0 choices
Identical nonrepeating strings have 1 choice
115.complexity: O(mn) time and O(mn) space, reducible to O(n) by updating target indices backward. Generalized counts can require arbitrary-precision integers.

72.summary: Find the fewest single-character insertions, deletions, or replacements needed to turn one string into another.
72.approach: Compare suffix pairs in a DP table, using remaining length as the cost when one suffix is empty. Matching characters advance both indices for free; otherwise add one to the cheapest insertion, deletion, or replacement continuation.
edgeCases: Equal strings → 0
"horse", "ros" → 3
72.complexity: O(mn) time and O(mn) table space; distance-only computation can use O(min(m,n)) space.

312.summary: Choose a balloon-bursting order that maximizes coins, where each burst multiplies the balloon by its currently adjacent values.
312.approach: Solve intervals by choosing which balloon is burst last inside each interval. Its two boundary balloons then remain fixed, allowing the left and right subintervals to be optimized independently; add virtual boundary values of one.
312.complexity: O(n³) time and O(n²) interval-DP space.

10.summary: Match an entire string against a pattern where dot matches one character and star repeats the preceding element zero or more times.
10.approach: Memoize string and pattern positions. When the next pattern symbol is star, either skip the element-star pair or consume one matching character while staying on that pair; without star, advance both positions on a match.
edgeCases: "aa" versus "a" → false
"aa" versus "a*" → true
"ab" versus ".*" → true
10.complexity: O(|s|·|p|) time and memo/table space. This is full matching with a limited regex grammar, not a general regex engine.

53.summary: Find the greatest sum of any nonempty contiguous subarray.
53.approach: At each value, decide whether to extend the best subarray ending just before it or begin a new one. Track the greatest ending sum seen, initializing from a real element so an all-negative array still returns a nonempty answer.
53.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space using Kadane’s recurrence.

55.summary: Determine whether the last array position is reachable when each value gives the maximum forward jump from that position.
55.approach: Work backward with a current goal index known to reach the end. Whenever an earlier position can jump to that goal, move the goal there; success means the goal eventually reaches index zero.
edgeCases: [0] → true
[0,1] → false
55.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space; zero values may block progress unless an earlier jump crosses them.

45.summary: Find the minimum number of forward jumps needed to reach the final array position, assuming it is reachable.
45.approach: Treat all positions reachable with the current number of jumps as one BFS layer represented by an index interval. Scan that interval to find the farthest next reach, then advance to the next layer and increment the jump count.
edgeCases: One position → 0 jumps
45.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space because each index is scanned in one layer; unreachable inputs need an extra no-progress guard outside the stated contract.

134.summary: Find a starting station that permits a full circular trip using each station’s gas and each outgoing leg’s cost, or report impossibility.
134.approach: The total gas must cover the total cost. In a forward scan, whenever the running tank becomes negative, discard every start in that failed segment and restart immediately after it; the surviving start works when the total balance is nonnegative.
edgeCases: One station with gas below cost → -1
Equal gas and cost at the only station → 0
A valid start can occur after a long initial deficit
134.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space; the total-balance check is necessary for the reset-on-deficit strategy.

846.summary: Determine whether a multiset of cards can be divided into equal-sized groups of consecutive values.
846.approach: Always start a group with the smallest remaining card, because no earlier group can absorb it later. Consume one occurrence of every required consecutive value and fail immediately if a value is missing or exhausted out of order.
edgeCases: Card count not divisible by group size → false
Group size 1 always succeeds
[1,2,3,3,4,5], group size 3 → true
846.complexity: O(n log u) time and O(u) space with a heap or sorted distinct keys, where u is the number of distinct card values.

1899.summary: Determine whether repeated coordinatewise-maximum merges of supplied triples can produce a target triple.
1899.approach: Discard every triple that exceeds the target in any coordinate, since a maximum merge can never undo that excess. Among the remaining triples, require that each target coordinate is reached by at least one triple; merging those witnesses achieves the target.
edgeCases: A triple exactly equal to target suffices
A matching coordinate in an oversized triple cannot be used
Three different valid triples may supply the three coordinates
1899.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space for fixed-size triples.

763.summary: Split a string into as many contiguous parts as possible so each character occurs in only one part.
763.approach: Record the last index of every character. While scanning a part, extend its required end to the latest last occurrence seen, and cut exactly when the scan reaches that end.
edgeCases: "aaaa" → one part of length 4
763.complexity: O(n) time and O(u) last-position space plus output; u is at most 26 for the stated alphabet.

678.summary: Check whether a string can become balanced parentheses when each star may stand for an opener, a closer, or nothing.
678.approach: Track the smallest and largest feasible count of unmatched opening parentheses for each prefix. Reject if even the largest count becomes negative, clamp the smallest at zero, and accept only if zero remains feasible at the end.
edgeCases: "*" → true
")*" → false
678.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space; the interval of possible balances replaces exponential assignment search.

57.summary: Insert one closed interval into a sorted nonoverlapping interval list, merging any overlaps.
57.approach: Copy intervals strictly before the new one, merge every interval that touches or overlaps it, and append the remaining intervals afterward. The existing ordering means no sorting is needed.
edgeCases: Empty input → the new interval alone
A new interval can cover the entire list
[1,2] and new [2,3] merge to [1,3]
57.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output; O(1) working state apart from output.

56.summary: Combine a collection of closed intervals so every overlapping region is represented once.
56.approach: Sort intervals by start point and keep the latest output interval open for extension. Merge when the next start is at most that interval’s end; otherwise begin a new output interval.
edgeCases: Unsorted disjoint intervals must be returned in order
56.complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) output plus sorting workspace; sorting and merging in place may mutate the input intervals.

435.summary: Remove the fewest intervals so the remaining intervals do not overlap, allowing one to end exactly when another begins.
435.approach: Keep the compatible intervals with the earliest possible finishing time. When a new interval overlaps the kept one, remove one and retain the smaller end, leaving maximum room for future intervals.
edgeCases: [1,2] and [2,3] need no removal
Three identical intervals require two removals
A long containing interval may be the best one to discard
435.complexity: O(n log n) time for sorting; O(1) scan space plus sorting workspace.

252.summary: Check whether one person can attend every scheduled meeting without a time conflict.
252.approach: Sort meetings by starting time and compare each meeting with the preceding one. A meeting conflicts only if it starts before the previous meeting ends, so touching endpoints are allowed.
edgeCases: No meetings → true
[1,2] followed by [2,3] → true
[1,4] and [2,3] → false
252.complexity: O(n log n) time and sorting-dependent extra space; the subsequent scan is O(n).

253.summary: Find the minimum number of rooms needed to host all meetings without conflicts within a room.
253.approach: Sort start times and end times separately, then sweep through their events. Allocate a room for a start before the next end, and free a room before processing a simultaneous start; the peak occupancy is the answer.
edgeCases: No meetings → 0 rooms
Back-to-back meetings can share one room
Three simultaneous meetings need three rooms
253.complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space for the sorted start/end arrays.

1851.summary: For each query value, find the length of the smallest closed interval containing it, or -1 if none does.
1851.approach: Sort queries and interval starts, then add all intervals whose start is at most the current query to a min heap keyed by length. Discard expired heap tops and read the shortest remaining candidate, finally restoring the original query order.
edgeCases: [4,4] has length 1 and contains query 4
Repeated queries must receive repeated answers
A query beyond every interval → -1
1851.complexity: O(n log n + q log q + (n+q) log n) time and O(n+q) space; interval length is end-start+1.

48.summary: Rotate a square matrix 90 degrees clockwise in place.
48.approach: Process the matrix layer by layer and rotate each group of four symmetric positions with one saved value. Alternatively, transpose across the main diagonal and reverse each row, preserving the same in-place mapping.
edgeCases: A 1×1 matrix is unchanged
An odd-sized matrix leaves its center in place
48.complexity: O(n²) time and O(1) extra space for an n×n matrix.

54.summary: Return every matrix value in clockwise spiral order starting from the top-left corner.
54.approach: Maintain top, bottom, left, and right boundaries for the unvisited rectangle. Traverse its four sides while shrinking the corresponding boundaries, rechecking validity before the bottom and left passes to avoid duplicate visits.
edgeCases: One row is emitted once from left to right
One column is emitted once from top to bottom
A 3×3 matrix ends at its center
54.complexity: O(RC) time, O(1) working state, and O(RC) output.

73.summary: If an original matrix cell is zero, set its entire row and column to zero in place.
73.approach: Use the first row and column as markers for which other rows and columns must be cleared. Preserve separate information for the first row or column, and apply the markers only after the complete discovery pass.
edgeCases: A zero in the first row needs separate handling
A zero at [0,0] affects both marker dimensions
A newly written zero must not trigger additional rows
73.complexity: O(RC) time and O(1) extra space with in-matrix markers.

202.summary: Determine whether repeatedly replacing a positive integer by the sum of its squared decimal digits eventually reaches one.
202.approach: The repeated transformation either reaches one or enters a cycle. Use slow and fast transformed values to detect the cycle without storing every prior number, then check whether their meeting value is one.
edgeCases: 1 → true
19 → true
2 enters a non-one cycle → false
202.complexity: O(log n) digit work to enter a bounded state range, then bounded-cycle work for fixed-width inputs; O(1) auxiliary space with Floyd’s method.

66.summary: Increment a nonnegative integer represented as an array of decimal digits.
66.approach: Work from the final digit toward the front, propagating a carry only through nines. Stop after incrementing a non-nine digit, or add a leading one if the carry survives every digit.
66.complexity: O(n) worst-case time; O(1) auxiliary space when updating digits in place, excluding a possible expanded output. Reversing into separate arrays instead uses O(n) space.

50.summary: Compute a real number raised to an integer power, including negative exponents.
50.approach: Use exponentiation by squaring: each halving of the exponent replaces two equal multiplications by one square. Accumulate the extra factor for odd exponents and take the reciprocal for a negative exponent, without overflowing when negating a minimum-width integer.
edgeCases: Any permitted nonzero base to exponent 0 → 1
2 to exponent -2 → 0.25
A negative base with odd exponent keeps a negative sign
50.complexity: O(log |n|) multiplications; O(log |n|) recursive space or O(1) iteratively. Floating-point rounding and underflow still apply.

43.summary: Multiply two nonnegative integers given as decimal strings without converting the entire inputs to numeric values.
43.approach: Accumulate each pair of digit products into its corresponding output position, just as in long multiplication. Normalize carries and remove leading zero positions, returning a single zero when either input is zero.
43.complexity: O(mn) time and O(m+n) space for digit arrays and output.

2013.summary: Store added points and count how many positive-area axis-aligned squares can use a queried point as one corner.
2013.approach: Track the multiplicity of every stored coordinate. For each possible opposite diagonal point, require equal nonzero horizontal and vertical distances, then multiply the counts at the two remaining corners and account for the diagonal point’s multiplicity.
edgeCases: Repeated added points multiply the number of square choices
Points sharing the query’s x or y are not diagonals
The query point need not have been added
2013.complexity: Expected O(1) add; count O(P) when scanning stored point occurrences for P added points, including duplicates; O(P) storage. Iterating unique coordinates can use O(U) per query.

136.summary: Find the only value appearing once when every other array value appears exactly twice.
136.approach: XOR every value into one accumulator. Equal pairs cancel and zero leaves the remaining value unchanged, so the final accumulator is the singleton.
136.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space under fixed-width integers; JavaScript Number bitwise operations use signed 32-bit values.

191.summary: Count the set bits in an unsigned binary integer.
191.approach: Repeatedly clear the lowest set bit with n AND (n-1). Each iteration removes exactly one one-bit, so counting iterations gives the population count.
edgeCases: A power of two → 1
Unsigned 32-bit all-ones value → 32
191.complexity: O(s) iterations for s set bits and O(1) fixed-width space; at most 32 iterations in the 32-bit version.

338.summary: Return the population count of every integer from zero through n.
338.approach: Reuse a smaller already-computed integer instead of counting each value from scratch. Removing the highest set power of two adds one bit to the earlier result, or equivalently use bits[i>>1] plus the low bit.
edgeCases: At each power of two, the new count resets to 1
338.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space, with O(1) extra state.

190.summary: Reverse all 32 bit positions of an unsigned integer, including leading zeros.
190.approach: Read each input bit and place it at the mirrored position, or shift an output accumulator while consuming input bits. Perform exactly 32 steps so low bits move into leading positions rather than stopping when the input becomes zero.
edgeCases: 0 remains 0
1 becomes 2^31
A set top bit becomes 1
190.complexity: O(32) time and O(1) space; in JavaScript normalize the returned Number with unsigned semantics when the top bit is set.

268.summary: Find the one value missing from an array containing distinct values drawn from zero through n.
268.approach: Cancel the observed values against the expected range using a running arithmetic difference or XOR of indices and values. Include n as well as indices zero through n-1 so a missing endpoint is handled correctly.
268.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space; arithmetic needs sufficient range, while XOR requires suitable fixed-width integer semantics.

371.summary: Add two signed integers without using addition or subtraction operators for the arithmetic.
371.approach: XOR combines bits without carrying, while shifted AND identifies the carry bits still to add. Repeat until no carry remains; for languages with unbounded signed integers, explicitly control the bit width or handle signs so negative carries terminate.
edgeCases: 0 plus a value returns that value
Opposite equal values sum to 0
Negative plus negative preserves the negative result
371.complexity: O(w) carry rounds and O(1) fixed-width space for w-bit integers; JavaScript bitwise Numbers use 32-bit two’s complement.

7.summary: Reverse an integer’s decimal digits while preserving its sign, returning zero if the result leaves the signed 32-bit range.
7.approach: Extract one signed decimal digit at a time and append it to the reversed accumulator. Before multiplying by ten and appending, check the positive or negative boundary so the implementation does not rely on an overflowing intermediate.
edgeCases: 1534236469 → 0 because the reversal overflows
7.complexity: O(log₁₀ |x|) time and O(1) space; division must truncate toward zero, and ±32-bit boundaries differ by one.

1929.summary: Create a new array containing two consecutive copies of an input sequence. Preserve the order within each copy.
1929.approach: Allocate an output of twice the input length and copy each value into its corresponding position in both halves. The first n output values and the final n values must each match the original.
edgeCases: One value must appear twice.
Repeated values retain their positions.
Verify that the input is unchanged.
1929.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space; O(1) extra working space beyond a preallocated result.

14.summary: Find the longest starting segment shared by every string in a collection.
14.approach: Compare characters at the same position across all strings. Stop at the first mismatch or when any string ends; everything before that position is proven common.
edgeCases: One string is a complete prefix of another.
One input string is empty.
The strings disagree at the first character.
14.complexity: O(mL) worst-case time for m strings and shortest length L; O(1) working space plus the returned prefix.

27.summary: Remove all occurrences of a chosen value by compacting the surviving values into the front of the same array. Return the meaningful prefix length.
27.approach: Keep a write index for the next retained value and scan with a separate read index. After every step, the written prefix contains exactly the values retained from the already scanned input; the unused suffix does not matter.
