edgeCases: Every value is removed, giving length zero.
No value matches the removal target.
Matches occur at both ends and between survivors.
27.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space; preserving survivor order is possible even when the contract does not require it.

169.summary: Identify the value occurring more than half the time in an array whose contract guarantees such a value exists.
169.approach: Use a candidate and a vote balance: equal values add a vote, different values cancel one, and a zero balance permits a new candidate. Pairwise cancellation cannot eliminate a strict majority; add a verification pass if the existence guarantee is removed.
edgeCases: The majority appears mainly near the end.
All values are identical.
A single value is the entire input.
169.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space; verification remains linear.

705.summary: Implement integer-set membership, insertion, and removal without using a built-in set.
705.approach: For a bounded key universe, a direct-address boolean array gives an especially clear implementation. Alternatively, hash into buckets and scan only a collision chain; deduplicate insertions and make removal of an absent key harmless.
edgeCases: Insert the same key twice.
Remove a key that was never inserted.
Use keys that collide in the chosen bucket function.
705.complexity: Direct addressing: O(1) operations and O(U) space for universe U. Resized chaining: expected O(1), worst-case O(n); a list-only implementation instead has O(n) operations.

706.summary: Implement a key-value map with replacement, lookup, and removal, including the required missing-key result.
706.approach: Hash each key to a bucket and store collision-chain entries containing both the key and value. Search for an existing key before appending; replacement changes its value, and deletion reconnects its neighbors.
edgeCases: Update an existing key without adding a second entry.
Remove the first or last item in a collision chain.
Look up a key after it has been removed.
706.complexity: Expected O(1 + n/b) per operation with b buckets; worst-case O(n). Space O(n+b); fixed bucket counts do not guarantee constant time as n grows.

912.summary: Sort an integer array without delegating the work to a built-in sorting function.
912.approach: Merge sort divides the range into halves, recursively sorts each half, and merges them with two read pointers. During merging, the output prefix always contains the smallest already consumed values in order.
edgeCases: The input is already sorted or reverse sorted.
Several values are equal.
Negative values and zero are mixed.
912.complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) merge storage, with O(log n) recursion depth; allocation details depend on the implementation.

75.summary: Rearrange an array containing three category codes so equal categories become consecutive in the required order.
75.approach: Maintain a low-category prefix, a high-category suffix, and an unclassified middle. Scan the middle: move low values left, high values right, and advance past middle values; after a swap from the right, classify the incoming value before advancing.
edgeCases: All entries belong to one category.
A swap from the right brings another high-category value.
The array contains only the first and last categories.
75.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space using a three-way partition.

304.summary: Preprocess an unchanging matrix so many inclusive rectangular-sum queries can be answered quickly.
304.approach: Build a padded two-dimensional prefix-sum table where each cell summarizes the rectangle above and to its left. A query combines four prefix values with inclusion-exclusion; padding removes special arithmetic for the top and left boundaries.
edgeCases: Query a single cell.
Query the full matrix or a rectangle touching an edge.
Include negative entries and a one-row matrix.
304.complexity: O(rows × columns) preprocessing time and space, followed by O(1) per query.

122.summary: Compute the greatest trading profit when any number of buy-sell pairs is allowed but at most one share can be held at a time.
122.approach: Add every positive change between consecutive prices. Each rising run telescopes to its valley-to-peak gain, so splitting that run into daily gains neither loses profit nor violates the one-share constraint.
edgeCases: Prices fall every day.
Several equal prices occur between rises.
There is only one price.
122.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space; this reasoning assumes no fee, cooldown, or transaction limit.

229.summary: Find every value that appears more than one third of the time. There can be at most two qualifying values.
229.approach: Extend majority voting to two candidate slots and counters, cancelling a triple of different values when both slots are occupied. Count the surviving candidates in a second pass, because cancellation alone does not prove that either exceeds the threshold.
edgeCases: Two distinct values both exceed n/3.
No value exceeds the threshold.
A value appears exactly n/3 times and must be excluded.
229.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, excluding an output of at most two values.

560.summary: Count contiguous, nonempty ranges whose values add to a chosen target, including inputs containing negative numbers.
560.approach: Track the running prefix sum and how often each earlier prefix occurred. A current sum s completes one range for every earlier prefix s−target; query before recording s so empty ranges are not counted.
edgeCases: Several zeroes create many distinct zero-sum ranges.
A matching range begins at index zero.
Negative values make a simple sliding window invalid.
560.complexity: Expected O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space with a hash map.

41.summary: Find the smallest positive integer absent from an unsorted array while using constant additional storage.
41.approach: Only values from 1 through n can affect the answer before n+1. Reuse array positions as presence markers, either by cyclic placement or carefully normalized sign marking; afterward, the first unmarked position identifies the missing value.
edgeCases: The array contains zero, negatives, and very large values.
Duplicate values must not cause repeated swaps forever.
Every integer from 1 through n is present.
41.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for in-place marking; a set-based alternative uses O(n) space.

344.summary: Reverse the order of characters in a mutable character array without creating a second array.
344.approach: Swap the leftmost and rightmost remaining characters, then move both pointers inward. The positions outside the pointers are final after each swap.
edgeCases: There is one character.
The length is odd, leaving a middle character untouched.
Repeated characters must still preserve correct positions.
344.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

680.summary: Decide whether a string can become a palindrome after deleting at most one character.
680.approach: Compare from both ends until the first mismatch. At that point the only useful choices are to skip the left character or the right character, then check the remaining interval without permitting another deletion.
edgeCases: The string is already a palindrome.
Only one of the two mismatch deletions works.
Two separated mismatches make one deletion insufficient.
680.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space with index-based checks; substring copies can add O(n) space.

1768.summary: Interleave two strings one character at a time, starting with the first string, then append any remainder.
1768.approach: Advance through both strings together while both have characters. Collect characters in a buffer and append the remaining suffix from the longer string before joining once.
edgeCases: One string is much longer than the other.
The strings have equal length.
Either string contains repeated characters.
1768.complexity: O(m+n) time and O(m+n) output space; repeated immutable-string concatenation may have worse copying costs.

88.summary: Merge two sorted sequences into the first array, which already has enough trailing capacity for both.
88.approach: Fill the destination from its final position backward, selecting the larger remaining value from either input. Writing backward prevents overwriting unread values in the first array; copy any remaining second-array values at the end.
edgeCases: The first sequence has no meaningful values.
All second-array values precede the first-array values.
Equal values appear in both arrays.
88.complexity: O(m+n) time and O(1) working space when copying element by element; slice-based variants allocate temporary storage.

26.summary: Compact a sorted array so each distinct value appears once in the returned prefix.
26.approach: The sorted order makes every duplicate adjacent to its first occurrence. Maintain a write position and copy only when the read value differs from the preceding distinct value.
edgeCases: All values are equal.
Every value is different.
Long duplicate runs occur at both ends.
26.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space; handle an empty array explicitly if extending beyond the original nonempty contract.

18.summary: Enumerate distinct value quadruples that sum to a target, using four different input positions.
18.approach: Sort the input, choose the first two positions, and solve the remaining two-sum with inward-moving pointers. Skip equal choices at each level and after a match so each value quadruple appears once.
edgeCases: Many duplicate values can produce the same quadruple.
The array contains fewer than four elements.
Use sums large enough to expose fixed-width overflow.
18.complexity: O(n³) time plus output storage; auxiliary sorting space depends on the language and sorting implementation.

189.summary: Rotate an array right by a given number of positions, modifying the existing array.
189.approach: Reduce the rotation count modulo the array length. Reverse the entire array, then reverse the two resulting segments independently to restore their internal order in their new positions.
edgeCases: The rotation count is zero or a multiple of the length.
The rotation count exceeds the length.
The input has one element; guard empty input in a generalized API.
189.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space with in-place reversals.

881.summary: Minimize the number of boats when each boat carries at most two people and has a fixed weight limit.
881.approach: Sort by weight and consider the heaviest remaining person, who must leave on the next boat. Pair that person with the lightest remaining person when they fit; otherwise the heaviest must travel alone.
edgeCases: The lightest and heaviest weights exactly meet the limit.
No pair can share a boat.
One person remains after the pointers meet.
881.complexity: O(n log n) time for sorting and O(n) for the scan; auxiliary sorting space is implementation-dependent.

219.summary: Determine whether two equal values occur within a specified maximum distance in array indices.
219.approach: Keep a set representing the preceding k positions and check each new value before adding it. Expire values that leave the allowed interval; an equal value in the set is a valid nearby duplicate.
edgeCases: k is zero, so distinct positions cannot qualify.
A duplicate is exactly k positions away.
A duplicate occurs just outside the allowed distance.
219.complexity: Expected O(n) time and O(min(n,k)) auxiliary space for a bounded-window set.

209.summary: Find the shortest contiguous block of positive numbers whose sum reaches a target, or report that none exists.
209.approach: Grow a window until its sum is large enough, then shrink from the left while it remains valid. Positivity guarantees that removing items never increases the sum and extending a too-small window is the only way forward.
edgeCases: One value alone reaches the target.
The entire array is still too small.
The best window appears at the final positions.
209.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space; allowing negative values requires a different argument and algorithm.

658.summary: Select k values nearest to a target from a sorted array, preferring the smaller value on equal distance and returning sorted output.
658.approach: The answer occupies a contiguous length-k window. Binary-search its starting index by comparing the value that would leave on the left with the value that would enter on the right; ties keep the left window.
edgeCases: The target lies outside the array range.
Distances tie on both sides of the target.
k equals the entire array length.
658.complexity: O(log(n−k+1) + k) time including output and O(k) output space; the search itself uses O(1) space.

682.summary: Evaluate a score history whose commands add a number, undo the last score, double it, or combine the last two scores.
682.approach: Use a stack for currently valid scores and translate each command into a local stack operation. Sum the surviving scores after processing, or maintain a running total consistently with every push and undo.
edgeCases: Undo removes a previously calculated score.
Scores can be negative.
A combine command uses the last two valid scores after earlier undos.
682.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space for n operations, assuming the input command sequence is valid.

225.summary: Implement last-in-first-out stack operations using queue operations as the underlying primitive.
225.approach: After enqueuing a new value, rotate all older values behind it so the newest value becomes the queue front. Pop and top can then use the front directly; explain the deliberate trade-off of expensive pushes.
edgeCases: Push after several pops.
Alternate one push and one pop repeatedly.
Check empty state after removing the final value.
225.complexity: O(n) push and O(1) pop/top with an O(1)-end-operation queue; O(n) storage. Array.shift in JavaScript can change these bounds.

232.summary: Implement a first-in-first-out queue using two last-in-first-out stacks.
232.approach: Push new items onto an input stack and serve removals from an output stack. Transfer all input items to the output stack only when the output is empty, reversing them into arrival order.
edgeCases: Push additional values while old output-stack items remain.
Peek must not remove an item.
Drain the queue completely and reuse it.
232.complexity: Amortized O(1) per operation and O(n) space; an individual transfer can cost O(n).

735.summary: Resolve collisions among signed moving objects on a line, keeping the survivors in their original spatial order.
735.approach: Keep survivors on a stack and process each new object against the stack top only when the top moves right and the newcomer moves left. Repeatedly remove the smaller magnitude, discard both on a tie, and continue until the newcomer is gone or no collision remains.
edgeCases: Equal magnitudes destroy each other.
One large left-moving object destroys several earlier objects.
Objects moving away from each other never collide.
735.complexity: O(n) amortized time and O(n) stack space, since each object is pushed and removed at most once.

901.summary: For each arriving price, report the number of consecutive ending days whose prices do not exceed the current price.
901.approach: Maintain a decreasing stack of price-and-span pairs. Pop every price no greater than the current one and add its already summarized span, then push the combined pair.
edgeCases: Equal prices extend the span.
Strictly falling prices all produce span one.
A late high price absorbs many earlier groups.
901.complexity: Amortized O(1) per arrival, O(n) total time and O(n) worst-case storage across n prices.

71.summary: Normalize an absolute Unix-style path using its syntactic navigation rules, without consulting the filesystem.
71.approach: Split into path components, ignore empty components and single dots, and pop one component for a double dot when possible. All other component names are literal; join the surviving stack beneath a single leading slash.
edgeCases: Repeated slashes and trailing slashes occur.
Parent steps attempt to move above the root.
Names such as three dots remain ordinary directory names.
71.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space for a path of n characters; this is syntactic normalization, not symlink resolution.

394.summary: Expand a nested repetition encoding into its decoded string.
394.approach: Use stack frames containing the outer text and repeat count when entering a bracketed region. On a closing bracket, finish the inner text, repeat it, and attach it to its parent; parse multi-digit counts rather than treating each digit independently.
edgeCases: A count has more than one digit.
Repetitions nest several levels deep.
Literal text appears before and after a repeated group.
394.complexity: At least O(L) time and space for decoded output length L. Repeated copying at nesting depth d can cost O(n+dL); avoid claims of linear time for naive concatenation.

895.summary: Build a stack-like structure that removes the most frequent value, breaking frequency ties by the most recent relevant push.
895.approach: Track each value’s current frequency and maintain a stack of values for each attained frequency. Push into the new-frequency stack; pop from the highest nonempty frequency stack, then lower that value’s count and update the maximum.
edgeCases: Two values share the highest frequency.
Popping changes which value is now most frequent.
Push a value again after its frequency has fallen.
895.complexity: Expected O(1) push/pop and O(n) stored push records, using hash maps and stacks.

35.summary: Find the index where a target occurs or would be inserted to preserve sorted order.
35.approach: Binary-search the first position whose value is at least the target using a half-open interval. Values strictly below the target leave the search on the left, and all other values remain candidates on the right.
edgeCases: The target precedes every existing value.
The target follows every existing value.
The target equals a boundary value.
35.complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

374.summary: Locate a hidden integer in a bounded range using only a comparison oracle that says lower, higher, or correct.
374.approach: Maintain the inclusive interval still compatible with all oracle responses. Probe its midpoint and discard the impossible half, carefully matching the oracle’s sign convention to the bound update.
edgeCases: The hidden value is the first or last permitted integer.
The range contains only one possibility.
A midpoint calculation must not overflow a fixed-width integer.
374.complexity: O(log n) oracle calls and O(1) auxiliary space.

69.summary: Compute the integer floor of a nonnegative number’s square root without using a square-root routine.
69.approach: Binary-search for the largest integer whose square does not exceed the input. Treat equality as valid and retain the best lower candidate; compare through division if squaring risks overflow.
edgeCases: The input is zero or one.
The input is one below or one above a perfect square.
A large input stresses multiplication overflow.
69.complexity: O(log(x+1)) time and O(1) auxiliary space under fixed-width arithmetic.

1011.summary: Find the smallest ship capacity that can transport ordered package weights within a day limit, without splitting packages.
1011.approach: For any proposed capacity, greedily load each day until the next package would exceed it. The required day count decreases monotonically as capacity grows, so binary-search between the heaviest package and the total weight.
edgeCases: Only one shipping day is available.
The day limit permits one package per day.
A package exactly fills the current day’s capacity.
1011.complexity: O(n log S) time and O(1) auxiliary space, where S is total weight.

81.summary: Search a rotated sorted array that may contain duplicate values and report whether the target is present.
81.approach: Use binary search when one half is demonstrably ordered, then test whether the target belongs within that half’s value bounds. If equal boundary and midpoint values hide the rotation, discard an ambiguous equal boundary carefully rather than assuming which half is sorted.
edgeCases: All values are equal but differ from the target.
Duplicates hide the rotation pivot.
The target occurs on both sides of the pivot.
81.complexity: O(log n) when useful halves can be discarded, but O(n) worst-case with duplicates; O(1) auxiliary space.

410.summary: Split a nonnegative array into a fixed number of nonempty contiguous pieces while minimizing the largest piece sum.
410.approach: Binary-search a candidate maximum sum and greedily count how many pieces are necessary to respect it. If at most k pieces suffice, nonnegative pieces can be split further to reach exactly k without increasing the maximum.
edgeCases: k is one or equals the number of values.
The input contains zeroes.
One very large value determines the lower bound.
410.complexity: O(n log S) time and O(1) auxiliary space for total sum S; the monotone greedy argument relies on nonnegative values.

1095.summary: Find the earliest target index in an array that rises strictly to one peak and then falls, accessing values through a limited-call interface.
1095.approach: Find the peak with a binary search on adjacent values. Search the increasing side first to satisfy the earliest-index rule, then search the decreasing side with reversed comparisons; cache interface reads to avoid repeated calls.
edgeCases: The target is the peak value.
The target appears once on each side of the peak.
The target is absent despite lying between the minimum and maximum.
1095.complexity: O(log n) interface queries with careful caching and O(log n) cache space; respect the platform’s explicit query budget.

92.summary: Reverse only the linked-list segment between two given one-based positions, leaving the rest connected.
92.approach: Use a dummy predecessor so reversal at the head needs no special branch. Remember the node before the segment and the segment’s original first node, reverse the chosen links, then reconnect both ends.
edgeCases: The segment begins at the head.
The segment ends at the tail.
The two positions are equal.
92.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for iterative pointer rewiring.

622.summary: Implement a bounded FIFO queue with front/rear inspection and explicit full/empty behavior.
622.approach: Use a fixed array, a head index, and a count; derive the insertion position modulo capacity. The count distinguishes full from empty even when indices coincide, and unsuccessful operations must leave state unchanged.
edgeCases: Capacity is one.
Indices wrap around after alternating inserts and removals.
Insertion into a full queue and removal from an empty queue fail cleanly.
622.complexity: O(1) per operation and O(k) reserved storage for capacity k; a bounded linked-list implementation has the same operation bounds.

460.summary: Implement a cache that evicts the least frequently accessed key, using least recent use to break frequency ties.
460.approach: Combine a key-to-entry map with a doubly linked list for each frequency and track the smallest active frequency. A hit or update moves one entry to the next-frequency list; insertion evicts the oldest entry in the minimum-frequency list when full.
edgeCases: Capacity is zero.
Updating a key changes both its value and access frequency.
Several keys tie in frequency but differ in recency.
460.complexity: Expected O(1) get/put with hash maps and linked lists, and O(capacity) live-entry space; discard empty frequency buckets to avoid unbounded metadata.

94.summary: Return a binary tree’s values in left-subtree, node, right-subtree order.
94.approach: Use a stack to descend the left spine, then visit the popped node and continue into its right subtree. The stack holds ancestors whose own visit is waiting for their left subtree to finish.
edgeCases: The tree is empty.
All nodes form one left or right chain.
Repeated values must not be deduplicated.
94.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) stack space for height h, plus O(n) output.

144.summary: Return a binary tree’s values with each parent appearing before its left and right subtrees.
144.approach: Visit a node immediately, then traverse its left subtree before its right subtree. In an explicit LIFO stack, push the right child before the left child so the left is processed first.
edgeCases: The root has only a right child.
The tree is empty.
A deep chain tests recursion depth limits.
144.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) traversal stack space, plus O(n) output.

145.summary: Return a binary tree’s values only after both child subtrees have been processed.
145.approach: Use recursive postorder or explicit stack entries that record whether a node is being entered or revisited. On entry, schedule the parent’s later visit and both children; append the parent only on the revisit.
edgeCases: The tree contains only a root.
One subtree is missing.
A skewed tree creates maximum traversal depth.
145.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) traversal stack space for a depth-first implementation, plus O(n) output.

701.summary: Insert a new value into a binary search tree while maintaining its ordering property, and return the resulting root.
701.approach: Compare the value with the current node and follow only the appropriate child link. Attach a new leaf at the first missing link; if the original root is absent, the new leaf becomes the root.
edgeCases: The starting tree is empty.
The new value becomes the smallest or largest key.
A skewed tree behaves like a linked list.
701.complexity: O(h) time; O(h) recursive stack or O(1) iterative working space. An unbalanced tree can have h=n.

450.summary: Delete a key from a binary search tree while preserving the ordering and reconnecting the remaining nodes.
450.approach: Find the key using the tree’s order. Replace a node with its only child when it has fewer than two children; otherwise use the next larger key from the right subtree and then delete that successor from its original position.
edgeCases: The key is absent.
The deleted node is the root or a leaf.
The successor has a right child that must remain connected.
450.complexity: O(h) time and O(h) recursive stack space; h may be n for an unbalanced tree.

427.summary: Represent a binary square grid as a quadtree whose leaves describe uniform regions.
427.approach: For each region, determine whether all cells share a value; if so, create one leaf. Otherwise split into four quadrants and build their children recursively, keeping quadrant positions consistent; a two-dimensional prefix sum can test uniformity in constant time.
edgeCases: The entire grid is uniform.
Only one cell differs from the rest.
A checkerboard forces subdivision down to individual cells.
427.complexity: Repeated region scans cost O(n² log n) worst-case. Prefix sums reduce construction to O(n²) time with O(n²) preprocessing/output space; recursion depth is O(log n).

337.summary: Choose tree nodes of maximum total value subject to never choosing a node together with its parent.
337.approach: Return two values from each subtree: the best total when its root is selected and when it is skipped. Selecting the root requires skipping both child roots; skipping it permits the better state independently from each child.
edgeCases: A large root competes with valuable children.
Grandchildren collectively outweigh their grandparents.
The tree is a single node or a long chain.
337.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space when each subtree is evaluated once.

1325.summary: Remove every leaf matching a target value, including new matching leaves exposed by earlier removals.
1325.approach: Process both children before deciding the current node’s fate. Once their updated links are attached, return null only if the current node is now a leaf with the target value; this single postorder pass handles cascading deletions.
edgeCases: Deleting children turns their matching parent into a removable leaf.
The root itself eventually disappears.
A matching internal node retains a nonmatching descendant.
1325.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space.

1834.summary: Simulate a processor that chooses the shortest available task, breaking ties by original task index, and return its execution order.
1834.approach: Sort tasks by release time and place available tasks in a min-heap keyed by duration and original index. After each completion, add newly released tasks; if no task is available, jump directly to the next release time.
edgeCases: The processor is idle between task batches.
Several tasks have the same processing time.
Tasks arrive while a long task is running.
1834.complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) auxiliary space; accumulated simulation time may require a wider integer type.

767.summary: Rearrange a string so equal characters never occupy adjacent positions, or report that no arrangement exists.
767.approach: Count remaining characters and repeatedly select the most frequent eligible character. Temporarily withhold the previously used character from the max-heap, returning it only after another character is chosen; if only the withheld character remains, completion is impossible.
edgeCases: One character occurs more than half the rounded-up length.
All characters are distinct.
A valid result exists exactly at the frequency feasibility boundary.
767.complexity: O(n log σ) time with σ distinct characters and O(σ) heap state plus O(n) output; use a buffer to avoid quadratic string copying.

1405.summary: Build the longest possible string from three available character counts while avoiding any run of three equal characters.
1405.approach: Prefer the character with the largest remaining count unless it would create a forbidden triple. In that case, use the best available different character; stop only when no valid next character exists, and reinsert unused counts after each choice.
edgeCases: Only one character has a positive count.
One count greatly exceeds the other two combined.
The final two output characters already match the most abundant character.
1405.complexity: O(a+b+c) time for a fixed three-character alphabet and O(1) working state, plus output; immutable concatenation can add copying overhead.

1094.summary: Check whether a vehicle can satisfy scheduled pickups and drop-offs without exceeding its capacity.
1094.approach: Sort trips by pickup position and keep active trips in a min-heap ordered by drop-off position. Before processing a pickup, release everyone whose trip has already ended, then add the new passengers and verify the load.
edgeCases: A drop-off and pickup happen at the same position.
Several trips overlap at the capacity limit.
One trip alone exceeds capacity.
1094.complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) heap space; bounded-coordinate difference arrays offer an alternative O(n+U) approach.

502.summary: Choose at most k affordable projects to maximize final capital, where completing a project increases capital by its profit.
502.approach: Order projects by required capital and move all currently affordable projects into a max-profit heap. Take the best affordable profit, update capital, and repeat; nonnegative profits ensure this greedy choice cannot reduce later affordability.
edgeCases: No project is initially affordable.
k exceeds the number of projects.
Several projects unlock only after an earlier profit is earned.
502.complexity: O(n log n + k log n) time with each project moved once, and O(n) auxiliary space; stop early when no affordable project remains.

1863.summary: Add the XOR value of every subset of an integer array, counting subsets by selected positions.
1863.approach: For each bit that appears in any value, exactly half of all subsets have that bit set in their XOR: pair subsets by toggling one position containing the bit. Therefore combine all present bits with OR and multiply by 2^(n−1); explicit include/exclude recursion is a useful baseline.
edgeCases: All values are zero.
Duplicate values still represent separate selectable positions.
A one-element array has only one nonzero-contributing subset.
1863.complexity: O(n) fixed-width bit operations and O(1) space for the identity; generalized large integers require accounting for bit width and result size.

77.summary: List every selection of k distinct numbers from the range 1 through n, without treating different orders as different answers.
77.approach: Build each selection in increasing order and recurse only on later candidate values. Prune a branch when the remaining values cannot fill its unoccupied positions, and copy the completed selection before backtracking.
edgeCases: k equals n.
k is one.
Near the end of the range, too few candidates remain to complete a branch.
77.complexity: Output alone costs Θ(k × C(n,k)); O(k) recursion/path space beyond output, with pruning avoiding fruitless branches.

47.summary: Generate each distinct permutation of a multiset exactly once.
47.approach: Count how many copies of each value remain and choose only values with a positive count. Decrement before recursion and restore afterward; choosing by value rather than by duplicate positions prevents repeated output permutations.
edgeCases: All input values are identical.
Two or more values have repeated occurrences.
A single value forms one permutation.
47.complexity: Output-sensitive exponential time, bounded by O(n × n!); O(n+u) working space for path/counts, excluding output, with u distinct values.

473.summary: Decide whether every available matchstick can be assigned to four sides of equal total length.
473.approach: Reject totals not divisible by four and sticks longer than the required side. Assign larger sticks first to one of four partially filled sides, backtracking on overflow; skip equivalent side totals to avoid exploring symmetric states.
edgeCases: The total length is not divisible by four.
A single stick exceeds the intended side length.
Many identical sticks create symmetric assignments.
473.complexity: O(4^n) worst-case search plus sorting, with O(n) recursion space; symmetry and descending-order pruning improve practical behavior.

698.summary: Partition all positive values into k nonempty groups with identical sums.
698.approach: First check divisibility and the largest-value bound. A bitmask DP can record the current bucket’s partial sum for each used-position mask: add an unused value only if it fits, and reset the partial sum to zero whenever a bucket is completed.
edgeCases: k is one or equals the number of values.
The total is divisible but no valid partition exists.
Repeated values create many equivalent choices.
698.complexity: O(n × 2^n) time and O(2^n) space for bitmask DP; backtracking alternatives instead have exponential search with different pruning costs.

52.summary: Count placements of n queens on an n-by-n board such that no pair attacks another.
52.approach: Place exactly one queen per row and track occupied columns plus both diagonal identifiers. Recurse only into unoccupied combinations and remove each placement on return; reaching row n contributes one complete board.
edgeCases: n is one.
Small board sizes have no valid placement.
Two distant cells can still share a diagonal.
52.complexity: Exponential search: O(n × n!) is a conservative bound for scanning n columns per partial placement; O(n) working space with column/diagonal sets.

140.summary: Produce every dictionary-word segmentation of a string, allowing dictionary words to be reused.
140.approach: Use suffix indices as subproblems and explore dictionary matches starting at each index. Memoize the possible suffix completions or first compute feasible suffixes to prune dead ends, then join words only when constructing an answer.
edgeCases: A prefix has several valid dictionary choices.
The final suffix cannot be segmented.
A word must be reused more than once.
140.complexity: Output can be exponential; include the total returned text size L in the bound. Trie-based match discovery is O(n·w), but materializing cached combinations can require much more time/space.

2707.summary: Cover a string with nonoverlapping dictionary matches while minimizing the number of uncovered characters.
2707.approach: Let dp[i] be the smallest uncovered count for the suffix starting at i. Either skip that character at cost one or follow a trie to each dictionary word ending later and take its suffix cost without an added penalty.
edgeCases: No dictionary word appears in the string.
A longer local match blocks a better overall cover.
Uncovered characters occur between two valid matches.
2707.complexity: O(D + n·w) time and O(D+n) space with a trie, where D is total dictionary length and w is the longest word length.

463.summary: Measure the boundary length of an island represented by occupied cells in a rectangular grid.
463.approach: Give each occupied cell four sides, then subtract two for every shared edge with an occupied neighbor already examined. A traversal alternative counts a boundary whenever it steps from land into water or outside the grid.
edgeCases: One isolated occupied cell contributes four sides.
Two adjacent cells share an internal edge.
Land touches the outer boundary of the matrix.
463.complexity: O(rows × columns) time and O(1) working space for direct edge counting; a traversal variant uses visited state and potentially linear recursion space.

953.summary: Check whether a sequence of words is sorted according to a supplied character ordering.
953.approach: Map each character to its rank and compare each neighboring pair of words. The first unequal character determines order; if all compared characters agree, the shorter word must come first.
edgeCases: A longer word precedes its exact prefix.
Adjacent words are identical.
Only a late character determines the ordering.
953.complexity: O(T + A) time for total compared characters T and alphabet size A; O(A) rank-map space.

997.summary: Identify a person trusted by everyone else who trusts nobody, or report that no such person exists.
997.approach: For each directed trust edge, subtract one from its source’s balance and add one to its destination’s balance. Under the distinct-edge contract, only a person with balance n−1 can have every required incoming edge and no outgoing edge.
edgeCases: There is one person and no trust edges.
A popular person trusts somebody else.
No person receives trust from every other person.
997.complexity: O(n+e) time and O(n) space for e trust edges; if duplicate edges are permitted, deduplicate before using this balance test.

752.summary: Find the fewest wheel turns needed to reach a combination while never entering forbidden combinations.
752.approach: Treat each combination as a graph vertex and each single-wheel increment or decrement as an edge. Breadth-first search from the initial combination gives minimum turns; exclude forbidden vertices and mark states when enqueued.
edgeCases: The initial combination is forbidden.
The target equals the initial combination.
Wheel rotation wraps between nine and zero.
752.complexity: For four decimal wheels, at most 10,000 states with eight neighbors each: O(10⁴ + d) time/space including d forbidden entries, treating four-character operations as constant.

1462.summary: Answer whether one course is a direct or indirect prerequisite of another for many queries.
1462.approach: Precompute reachability rather than repeating a full traversal for every query. A clear baseline uses a boolean transitive-closure matrix: for each possible intermediate course, connect every predecessor to every successor, then answer each query by lookup.
edgeCases: A prerequisite chain contains several intermediate courses.
Two courses are unrelated.
One course is a prerequisite through multiple different paths.
1462.complexity: O(v³ + q) time and O(v²) space for closure and q queries; DAG-specific propagation can improve this, while memoized set unions have different costs.

721.summary: Merge account records linked by shared email addresses, preserving the owner name and returning sorted unique emails per component.
721.approach: Map each email to the first account that contains it and union any later account sharing that email. Group emails by the final component representative, deduplicate through the email map, and sort each component’s emails before formatting the result.
edgeCases: Two records have the same name but share no email.
An account bridges two previously separate groups.
The same email appears in several records.
721.complexity: Near-linear union-find work plus O(E log E) worst-case email sorting, with O(A+E) space for A accounts and E distinct emails; string comparison costs depend on email length.

399.summary: Use known variable ratios to answer division queries, reporting when no relationship can be established.
399.approach: Build a weighted graph with one edge for each ratio and its reciprocal. For a query, traverse from the numerator to the denominator while multiplying weights; a missing variable or disconnected target has no answer.
edgeCases: A query uses a variable never seen in any equation.
A known variable divided by itself gives one.
The answer requires reversing or chaining several equations.
399.complexity: O(v+e) construction and O(q(v+e)) time for independent graph searches, with O(v+e) space; floating-point ratios require tolerant comparison.

310.summary: Find all roots that minimize the height of a given undirected tree.
310.approach: Tree centers remain after repeatedly removing all current leaves together. Track degrees, peel one layer at a time, and stop when at most two vertices remain; those vertices minimize the greatest distance to any other vertex.
edgeCases: The tree has one or two vertices.
A long path has one or two central roots.
A star-shaped tree has its hub as the only answer.
310.complexity: O(v+e) time and space, which is O(n) for a tree; the leaf-peeling argument assumes the input is connected and acyclic.

1631.summary: Choose a route across a height grid that minimizes its largest single-step height difference.
1631.approach: Use Dijkstra’s frontier, but combine a route cost with an edge using max rather than addition. An improved candidate is max(current effort, edge difference), and the first finalized destination has the smallest achievable worst step.
edgeCases: A one-cell grid needs no effort.
A longer route avoids one steep direct step.
Many routes share the same maximum edge cost.
1631.complexity: O(rc log(rc)) time and O(rc) state for an r-by-c grid with a lazy heap; discard stale heap entries to avoid unnecessary work.

1489.summary: Classify graph edges as required in every minimum spanning tree or usable in at least one such tree without being required.
1489.approach: Compute a baseline minimum spanning-tree weight with Kruskal’s algorithm. For each edge, recompute while excluding it to test necessity, then force it first and finish Kruskal to test whether a minimum-weight tree can contain it; keep original indices through sorting.
edgeCases: Several equal-weight edges can substitute for one another.
Removing an edge disconnects the graph.
An expensive edge belongs to no minimum spanning tree.
1489.complexity: O(e log e + e² α(v)) time when edges are sorted once and union-find is reused per trial; O(v+e) working storage plus output.

2392.summary: Place each value from 1 through k once in a square matrix so separate above/below and left/right constraints are satisfied.
2392.approach: Topologically sort the row constraints and the column constraints independently. A cycle in either makes placement impossible; otherwise each value receives its row position from the first order and its column position from the second, with all unused cells zero.
edgeCases: Only the row constraints contain a cycle.
Repeated precedence edges must be handled consistently.
Many values are unrelated and permit several valid layouts.
2392.complexity: O(k²+r+c) time including the output matrix, and O(k+r+c) working space plus O(k²) output for r row edges and c column edges.

2709.summary: Determine whether all array positions are connected when two positions may link whenever their values share a factor greater than one.
2709.approach: Factor each value and associate each prime factor with one previously seen index. Union indices that share a prime factor instead of checking every pair, then test whether all indices have the same representative.
edgeCases: A value of one is isolated unless it is the only input.
Equal values at different positions still need connectivity.
Values connect through a chain even when the endpoints have gcd one.
2709.complexity: Trial division gives O(n√M) factorization work plus near-linear union operations; space O(n+F) for F distinct factors. A smallest-prime-factor sieve offers a different time/memory trade-off.

1137.summary: Evaluate a sequence whose next value is the sum of its preceding three values, using the specified initial terms.
1137.approach: Handle the first three indices directly and keep only the last three values while advancing. A recursive solution needs memoization to avoid recomputing the same prefixes repeatedly.
edgeCases: Request each of the three initial terms.
The first computed term uses all initial values.
Larger indices expose exponential work in an unmemoized recursion.
1137.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) working space for iteration; a memoized recursive variant uses O(n) space.

377.summary: Count ordered sequences of allowed positive values that add to a target; different orders count separately.
377.approach: Let dp[t] count sequences totaling t, with one empty sequence for total zero. For each total in ascending order, consider every possible final value and add dp[t−value]; putting totals in the outer loop counts orderings correctly.
edgeCases: No value can contribute to the target.
Two values can be used in either order, producing different sequences.
Including zero or negative candidates would invalidate the finite positive-value recurrence.
377.complexity: O(target × m) time and O(target) space for m allowed values; large counts may require wider arithmetic.

279.summary: Express a positive integer as a sum of perfect squares using the fewest terms.
279.approach: Use dp[t] for the smallest number of squares totaling t, starting with dp[0]=0. Try each square no larger than t as the final term and take one plus the best remaining total.
edgeCases: The input is itself a perfect square.
Several small squares beat a greedy choice of the largest square.
The input is one.
279.complexity: O(n√n) time and O(n) space for the direct dynamic program; number-theoretic alternatives have different bounds.

343.summary: Split a positive integer into at least two positive parts so their product is as large as possible.
343.approach: For each total, consider a first part and compare leaving the remainder intact with splitting it further. Keep the best product and enforce the initial requirement of at least one split; a separate mathematical argument leads to mostly parts of three.
edgeCases: The smallest legal input still requires two parts.
A remainder of one makes a naive all-threes strategy suboptimal.
A part may be better left intact than split again.
343.complexity: O(n²) time and O(n) space for the direct DP; a proven factor-of-three strategy reduces the computation.

1406.summary: Determine the winner when two optimal players take one, two, or three consecutive values from the front and accumulate their signed values.
1406.approach: Let dp[i] be the largest score advantage the current player can force from suffix i. For each allowed take count, subtract the opponent’s best suffix advantage from the taken sum; the sign of dp[0] determines the winner or a tie.
edgeCases: All remaining values are negative.
Only one or two values remain.
Optimal play produces equal final scores.
1406.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) DP space, reducible to O(1) rolling state because only the next three states are needed.

63.summary: Count routes across a rectangular grid when movement is limited to right and down and some cells are blocked.
63.approach: Sweep the grid with a one-dimensional DP array. A blocked cell resets its path count to zero; an open cell receives paths from the previously stored vertical neighbor and the current horizontal neighbor.
edgeCases: The start or destination is blocked.
A complete blocked row separates start and destination.
The grid has only one row or column.
63.complexity: O(rows × columns) time and O(columns) auxiliary space; count size can matter outside the platform’s numeric guarantees.

64.summary: Find the minimum cost of a route from one corner of a weighted grid to the opposite corner, moving only right or down.
64.approach: For each cell, add its cost to the smaller reachable predecessor total. A row-compressed DP retains exactly the previous-row values and the already processed current-row neighbor, avoiding a full second matrix.
edgeCases: The grid has one cell.
There is only one row or one column.
The cheapest local next step is not on the globally cheapest route.
64.complexity: O(rows × columns) time and O(columns) auxiliary space; O(1) extra space is possible if input mutation is allowed.

1049.summary: Choose a sequence of pairwise stone reductions that leaves the smallest possible final weight.
1049.approach: View the reductions as assigning each original weight to one of two opposing totals. Find a reachable subset sum as close as possible to half the total, then minimize the difference between that sum and the remainder.
edgeCases: An exact equal partition leaves zero weight.
One stone is larger than all others combined.
Repeated weights must each be usable at most once.
1049.complexity: O(nS) time and O(S) space for a one-dimensional subset-sum DP with total weight S; memoized index-and-sum variants use O(nS) states.

877.summary: Determine whether the first player can win an optimal end-picking game with an even number of positive piles and an odd total.
877.approach: The first player can commit to taking all piles from either parity of their original indices. Choose the parity with the larger sum; the even pile count keeps that strategy enforceable, and the odd total prevents equal parity totals.
edgeCases: There are only two piles.
Large values cluster on one original-index parity.
If the count or odd-total guarantee is removed, the unconditional-win proof no longer applies.
877.complexity: O(1) answer under the stated guarantees; a general interval game DP costs O(n²) time and space.

1140.summary: Maximize the first player’s final stones when each turn takes a prefix of at most twice a stateful limit M, updating M to the larger of M and the number taken.
1140.approach: Memoize the best achievable total for a player at state (start,M). Using suffix sums, evaluate each legal take as the remaining total minus the opponent’s best response at the updated state; if all remaining piles fit, take them all.
edgeCases: The remaining suffix already fits within 2M.
Taking more now increases the opponent’s later limit.
A valuable pile lies just beyond the current reach.
1140.complexity: O(n³) time is a straightforward upper bound for O(n²) states each trying O(n) moves; O(n²) memo space plus recursion.

860.summary: Process customers in order and determine whether exact change can always be made for a fixed-price purchase using only cash already received.
860.approach: Track counts of the useful small bills. When a larger bill needs change, prefer a combination that uses the larger available change bill and preserves smaller bills, since smaller bills serve more future cases.
edgeCases: The first customer cannot receive the required change.
A large bill can be changed in two different ways.
A prior choice leaves too few small bills for a later customer.
860.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) state for the fixed denominations; this greedy choice does not generalize automatically to arbitrary currencies.

918.summary: Find the largest sum of a nonempty contiguous block when an array is considered circular and no position may be used twice.
918.approach: Compute the best ordinary subarray and the smallest ordinary subarray alongside the total sum. A wrapping answer is the total minus a minimum middle block; when every value is negative, use the ordinary maximum instead of accidentally selecting an empty complement.
edgeCases: All values are negative.
The best block wraps across the last and first positions.
The whole array is optimal or there is a single element.
918.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space using maximum and minimum Kadane scans.

978.summary: Find the longest contiguous interval whose neighboring comparisons alternate between rising and falling.
978.approach: Track the sign of the previous unequal comparison and the current alternating-run length. Extend only when the sign flips; equality resets the run to one, while a repeated sign starts a new two-element candidate.
edgeCases: Two adjacent values are equal.
The array is strictly increasing.
A long alternating run begins after an early reset.
978.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary state.

1871.summary: Determine whether the final position of a binary string is reachable by forward jumps within a given length interval, landing only on zeroes.
1871.approach: Let reachable[i] depend on whether any reachable predecessor lies from i−maxJump through i−minJump. Maintain the count of such predecessors as a sliding window, adding and expiring one position per step instead of checking every possible jump.
edgeCases: The final character is blocked.
minJump equals maxJump.
A valid predecessor leaves the window just before a later zero.
1871.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) reachability storage; a bounded circular buffer can reduce stored history when the maximum jump is small.

649.summary: Predict which faction wins a cyclic voting process when each active participant can remove an opponent from future turns.
649.approach: Keep each faction’s surviving turn positions in an increasing queue. Compare the two earliest positions: the earlier participant bans the other and returns at its position plus the cycle length, preserving chronological order for the next round.
edgeCases: Only one faction is present.
One faction has an early turn but fewer participants.
The decisive ban occurs after wrapping into another cycle.
649.complexity: O(n) queue operations and O(n) space with O(1) deque operations; repeated front removal from a plain array can make an implementation slower.

135.summary: Assign the fewest rewards so every child receives one and each child with a higher rating than a neighbor receives more than that neighbor.
135.approach: Initialize everyone to one, then scan left to right to satisfy rising comparisons with the left neighbor. Scan right to left to enforce the opposite constraint using the maximum of the existing assignment and the required right-neighbor value.
edgeCases: Neighboring ratings are equal and impose no strict ordering.
A long peak needs constraints from both directions.
The ratings are strictly decreasing.
135.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space for the two-pass method; a slope-counting alternative can use O(1) space.

2402.summary: Allocate meetings to numbered rooms, delaying a meeting when every room is busy, and report the room used most often with the specified index tie-break.
2402.approach: Process meetings by original start time, maintaining a min-heap of free room IDs and another of busy (finishTime,roomId) pairs. Release all rooms already free; if none is available, select the earliest finishing room and shift the meeting while preserving its duration.
edgeCases: Several rooms become free at the same instant.
A meeting starts exactly when another ends.
Delayed meetings accumulate times larger than original endpoints.
2402.complexity: O(m log m + m log r) time and O(r) heap/count state, excluding sorted input storage, for m meetings and r rooms; use sufficiently wide time arithmetic.

168.summary: Convert a positive spreadsheet column number into its alphabetic label, where the first position is A rather than a zero digit.
168.approach: Treat the label as a bijective base-26 representation. Subtract one before taking each remainder, map it to a letter, divide the adjusted number by 26, and reverse the collected letters.
edgeCases: The number is the last one-letter column.
The next number begins the two-letter labels.
A label ends in Z after carrying through earlier positions.
168.complexity: O(log₍₂₆₎ n) time and output space with buffered characters; naive repeated concatenation may add copying cost.

1071.summary: Find the longest string that can be repeated a whole number of times to form each of two given strings.
1071.approach: First verify that concatenating the strings in either order produces the same result; otherwise they have no common repeating base. When compatible, take a prefix whose length is the greatest common divisor of the two lengths.
edgeCases: The strings have compatible lengths but different repeated content.
One string is several copies of the other.
The common base contains more than one distinct character.
1071.complexity: O(m+n) time and O(m+n) temporary space for concatenation-based checking; a character-wise check can reduce working space. Checking every possible divisor length has a higher bound.

2807.summary: Insert a new linked-list node between every original adjacent pair, storing the greatest common divisor of that pair’s values.
2807.approach: Walk the original links and compute each pair’s gcd with Euclid’s algorithm. Save the original next node before insertion and advance to that node afterward so newly inserted nodes do not become inputs to the next pair.
edgeCases: The list contains only one node.
Adjacent values are coprime.
Equal adjacent values produce the same value in the inserted node.
2807.complexity: O(n log M) time for n original nodes and maximum value M, O(1) working space, and O(n) newly allocated output nodes.

867.summary: Transpose a rectangular matrix so each original row becomes an output column.
867.approach: Allocate an output with swapped dimensions and assign output[column][row] from input[row][column]. Keep the two dimensions separate; the matrix need not be square.
edgeCases: The input has one row.
The input has one column.
Rows and columns have different lengths as dimensions, while each input row remains rectangular.
867.complexity: O(rows × columns) time and output space; O(1) auxiliary space beyond the new matrix.

13.summary: Interpret a valid Roman numeral string as an integer, respecting subtractive pairs.
13.approach: Map each symbol to its value and inspect its next neighbor. Subtract the current value when it is smaller than the following value; otherwise add it, which accounts for each subtractive pair without consuming characters twice.
edgeCases: A subtractive pair appears at the start or end.
The numeral contains only repeated additive symbols.
A single symbol has no following character.
13.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for the fixed symbol alphabet; this assumes valid Roman-numeral input rather than implementing a validator.

67.summary: Add two binary numbers represented as strings without relying on a bounded integer conversion.
67.approach: Traverse both strings from right to left, combining available bits with a carry. Append each output bit to a reversed buffer, emit a final carry if needed, then reverse and join once.
edgeCases: The strings have unequal lengths.
A carry propagates through every existing bit.
Both numbers are zero.
67.complexity: O(max(m,n)) time and output space with buffered construction; repeated string prepending may be quadratic.

201.summary: Compute the bitwise AND of every integer in an inclusive nonnegative range without enumerating the entire range.
201.approach: Only the common high-bit prefix of the two endpoints can survive. Shift both endpoints right until they agree, count the shifts, then restore that shared prefix with zeroes in all changed lower positions.
edgeCases: Both endpoints are identical.
The range crosses a power-of-two boundary.
The lower endpoint is zero.
201.complexity: O(w) time and O(1) fixed-width working space for w-bit integers; JavaScript bitwise operators use signed 32-bit values, so wider variants need BigInt.

3133.summary: Minimize the final value of an increasing positive array of length n whose combined bitwise AND is x.
3133.approach: Every chosen value must include all set bits of x, so start with x and treat its zero-bit positions as free digits. Deposit the binary digits of n−1 into those zero positions from low to high; this selects the nth smallest permitted value without constructing the whole array.
edgeCases: n is one, so the answer is x.
The low bits of x are all set, forcing new bits higher up.
The result exceeds the safe range of 32-bit JavaScript bitwise arithmetic.
3133.complexity: O(log n + log x) bit-position steps with fixed-width arithmetic; use BigInt for wide JavaScript results and account for bit-operation cost with arbitrary precision.

6.summary: Simulate a character stream that travels down rows and then diagonally back up; read the completed rows in order.
6.approach: Keep one buffer per row and a direction flag. Append each character to the current row, reversing direction only at the first or last row; concatenate the buffers at the end.
edgeCases: One row: preserve the input.
More rows than characters: no rearrangement.
Two rows: alternate between them.
6.complexity: Target O(n) time and O(n + r) storage for n characters and r rows, using appendable buffers; repeated immutable concatenation may add copying.

9.summary: Determine whether an integer’s decimal digits read identically from both ends without converting it to text.
9.approach: Reject negative numbers and nonzero values ending in zero. Reverse only the lower half of the digits, then compare the two halves, discarding the middle digit for odd lengths.
edgeCases: 0 is a palindrome.
A negative value such as -121 fails.
120 fails despite its trailing zero.
9.complexity: O(log10 x) time and O(1) machine-word space; reversing half avoids building a potentially overflowing full reversal.

12.summary: Encode a positive integer using Roman numerals, including the special subtractive pairs.
12.approach: Process a descending table of values that includes pairs such as 900 and 40. Emit as many copies of the current symbol as fit, then continue with the remainder; including subtractive pairs makes the greedy choice canonical.
edgeCases: 4 needs IV rather than four I symbols.
A value like 940 uses two subtractive pairs.
3999 exercises thousands and upper-range digits.
12.complexity: O(L) time for output length L and O(L) output storage; the official bounded input range makes both bounded constants.

24.summary: Swap each adjacent pair of linked-list nodes by rewiring links while retaining the nodes themselves.
24.approach: Use a dummy predecessor to handle a swap at the head uniformly. Save the node after the pair, connect predecessor to second and second to first, then reconnect first to the saved suffix before advancing.
edgeCases: An empty list stays empty.
A singleton has no partner.
An odd-length list keeps its final node.
24.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space with iterative pointer updates.

28.summary: Locate the earliest occurrence of one string inside another, or report that it never occurs.
28.approach: Build a prefix-failure table for the pattern, then scan the text with a pattern pointer. On a mismatch, retain the longest usable matched prefix instead of moving the text pointer backward; the first complete match is the answer.
edgeCases: The pattern is longer than the text.
Repeated prefixes such as aaaaab stress fallback.
A match ends at the text’s last character.
28.complexity: KMP target: O(n + m) time and O(m) space. Trying every start directly can take O(nm).

30.summary: Find starting positions where a contiguous region consists of exactly the supplied equal-length words, in any order.
30.approach: Build the required word-frequency map and scan separately for every offset modulo the word length. Extend by one word at a time, clearing on an unknown word and shrinking when a word is overrepresented; record windows containing the required total number of words.
edgeCases: The word list contains duplicate words.
Several valid windows overlap.
The full concatenation is longer than the text.
30.complexity: With n text characters, word length w, and k words: O(nw + kw) time if slicing/hashing each token costs O(w); O(kw) key storage. Token operations can reduce the scan to O(n).

31.summary: Transform an array into its next lexicographic permutation, wrapping to the smallest arrangement when necessary.
31.approach: Find the rightmost position whose value is smaller than its successor. Swap it with the rightmost larger suffix value, then reverse the suffix, which was nonincreasing; if there is no pivot, reverse the whole array.
edgeCases: A fully descending array wraps around.
Repeated values require a strictly larger swap.
A one-element array is unchanged.
31.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space with in-place reversal.

32.summary: Measure the longest contiguous region of a parentheses string that forms a balanced expression.
32.approach: Keep a stack of unmatched opening indices with an initial boundary of -1. When closing a pair, the index remaining on top marks the boundary before the current valid region; an unmatched closing parenthesis becomes the new boundary.
edgeCases: An empty string has length zero.
All characters are opening parentheses.
Adjacent valid groups can combine into a longer region.
32.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) stack space; two directional counting passes can reach O(1) extra space.

34.summary: Find the first and last positions of a target within a sorted array containing possible duplicates.
34.approach: Perform two binary searches with different boundary biases. One searches for the first value at least the target, while the other searches for the first value greater than it; verify that the first boundary actually contains the target.
edgeCases: The target is absent.
Every value equals the target.
The only match is at an array endpoint.
34.complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) extra space; avoid scanning outward through duplicates.

58.summary: Count the characters in the final word while ignoring trailing spaces.
58.approach: Scan backward past the trailing spaces, then count until another space or the beginning is reached. This avoids allocating a complete list of words just to inspect the last one.
edgeCases: There are several trailing spaces.
The input contains one single-letter word.
Several spaces separate the final two words.
58.complexity: O(n) worst-case time and O(1) extra space with a reverse scan.

61.summary: Rotate a linked list to the right by k positions while reusing its nodes.
61.approach: Find the list length and reduce k modulo that length. Locate the new tail n-k nodes from the start, join the old tail to the old head, and cut the link after the new tail to restore a linear list.
edgeCases: An empty list must avoid modulo by zero.
k is a multiple of the list length.
k is much larger than the list length.
61.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space; remember to break the temporary cycle.

68.summary: Pack words into fixed-width lines and distribute spaces according to full-justification rules.
68.approach: Greedily take the largest group of words that fits with at least one space between neighbors. For ordinary lines, divide spare spaces among gaps and give the remainder to earlier gaps; a last line or a single-word line is left-aligned and padded on the right.
edgeCases: A line contains only one word.
Extra spaces do not divide evenly across gaps.
The final line fits fewer words than earlier lines.
68.complexity: O(total output characters) construction time with buffers, plus scanning the input; output storage is proportional to the padded lines.

80.summary: Compact a sorted array so each distinct value appears at most twice in its retained prefix.
80.approach: Maintain a write index for the valid prefix. Accept a value whenever fewer than two values have been written or it differs from the value two positions behind the write index; sorted order makes that comparison sufficient.
edgeCases: The array has fewer than three elements.
A run contains many copies of one value.
Every value is already distinct.
80.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space; only the returned-length prefix is meaningful.

82.summary: Remove every value that occurs more than once in a sorted linked list, leaving only unique values.
82.approach: Use a dummy node and a predecessor pointing to the last retained node. Scan an entire equal-value run before deciding: bypass the whole run if it repeats, otherwise advance the retained predecessor.
edgeCases: A duplicate run begins at the head.
Every node has the same value.
A repeated run occurs at the tail.
82.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space with iterative traversal.

86.summary: Rearrange a linked list around a threshold while preserving order within the smaller and remaining groups.
86.approach: Append each encountered node to one of two chains, based on whether its value is below the threshold. Terminate the second chain explicitly, then join the first chain to it; stable appends preserve relative order.
edgeCases: All nodes are below the threshold.
No nodes are below the threshold.
Values equal to the threshold belong in the second chain.
86.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space when reusing nodes.

101.summary: Check whether a binary tree has matching values and structure under a left-right reflection.
101.approach: Compare nodes in mirrored pairs, not by checking values at each depth alone. A pair succeeds when both are absent; otherwise their values must match and the outer and inner child pairs must both be symmetric.
edgeCases: A single root is symmetric.
Equal values hide a missing child on one side.
Mirrored branches have different values.
101.complexity: O(n) time; recursive comparison uses O(h) stack space, while a breadth-first queue can use O(width).

103.summary: Collect a tree’s levels while alternating the reading direction at each depth.
103.approach: Use breadth-first traversal and fix the current level size before processing it. Place values into a level buffer from the appropriate end, while always enqueuing children in a consistent order for the next level.
edgeCases: An empty tree produces no levels.
A one-sided tree still alternates direction.
A broad level contains repeated values.
103.complexity: Target O(n) time and O(width) auxiliary queue space, excluding output. Use a deque or head index; repeated front deletion from an array can become quadratic.

106.summary: Reconstruct a binary tree from its inorder and postorder traversal sequences.
106.approach: Index each value’s inorder position to split a subtree without searching. Consume postorder backward: the next value is the root, and its right subtree must be built before its left subtree because of the reversed traversal order.
edgeCases: The tree consists of one node.
A skewed tree reaches linear recursion depth.
The root has only a left or only a right subtree.
106.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) index-map storage plus O(h) recursion, assuming distinct values and index ranges rather than copied slices.

108.summary: Build a height-balanced search tree from an already sorted array.
108.approach: Choose the midpoint of each index range as the subtree root. Recursively build the lower and higher halves; nearly equal range sizes ensure balanced heights while sorted order establishes the search-tree property.
edgeCases: An even-length range permits two valid midpoint choices.
A one-element range creates a leaf.
Negative and positive values appear together.
108.complexity: Target O(n) time, O(log n) recursion, and O(n) output nodes using index bounds. Repeated array slicing adds O(n log n) copying work.

112.summary: Decide whether some complete root-to-leaf path adds up to a requested total.
112.approach: Carry a remaining sum down the tree, subtracting the current node’s value. Accept only when a leaf makes that remainder zero; reaching zero at an internal node does not finish a root-to-leaf path.
edgeCases: An empty tree has no qualifying path.
An internal prefix sums to the target but no leaf path does.
Negative values make early sum-based pruning unsafe.
112.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) depth-first stack space, with h potentially n.

114.summary: Rewire a binary tree into a right-linked chain following preorder traversal, clearing every left link.
114.approach: Walk the tree in preorder while moving each left subtree onto the right. When a left subtree exists, connect its rightmost node to the current right subtree before moving it; this preserves the postponed preorder suffix.
edgeCases: The tree is already a right-only chain.
The tree is a left-only chain.
Both subtrees must retain their relative preorder positions.
114.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space for iterative rewiring; a recursive implementation uses O(h) stack space.

117.summary: Link each node to its neighbor on the same level in a binary tree that may have missing children.
117.approach: Walk the current level using next pointers that were built in the previous round. A dummy head and tail collect its children into the next level’s chain, skipping missing children without assuming a perfect tree.
edgeCases: An empty tree needs no links.
A child must connect across several missing siblings.
The last node of every level must point to null.
117.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space with level-chain traversal; a normal BFS alternative uses O(width).

118.summary: Generate successive rows of Pascal’s triangle from their neighboring values in the preceding row.
118.approach: Start each new row with boundary values of one. Fill each interior position by adding the two values above it, then retain the completed row for both the answer and the next construction step.
edgeCases: One requested row produces only [1].
The second row has no interior positions.
Later rows must use the previous row rather than partially written values.
118.complexity: For r rows, O(r²) time and O(r²) required output space; O(r) temporary space suffices beyond the output.

120.summary: Find the least-cost downward route through a triangle, choosing between the two adjacent entries below each position.
120.approach: Work upward from the final row with a one-dimensional cost buffer. Each entry becomes its value plus the smaller of the two reachable costs beneath it, so each update summarizes the best suffix path.
edgeCases: A single-row triangle returns its sole value.
Negative entries can make locally expensive choices worthwhile.
The cheapest path can hug either edge.
120.complexity: O(r²) time and O(r) extra space for r rows; reusing the final row saves allocation but mutates the input.

123.summary: Maximize trading profit when at most two buy-then-sell transactions are allowed and holdings cannot overlap.
123.approach: Track the best balances after the first buy, first sale, second buy, and second sale. Update these states for each price using the previous day’s states, allowing a transaction to remain unused when it cannot improve profit.
edgeCases: Prices only decrease, so doing nothing is best.
A single price cannot produce a sale profit.
One long trade can beat splitting into two.
123.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) state for the fixed two-transaction limit.

129.summary: Interpret each root-to-leaf sequence of digit-valued nodes as a number and sum those numbers.
129.approach: Carry an integer prefix down the traversal, replacing it with prefix × 10 plus the current digit. Add the prefix only at a leaf so shared prefixes contribute separately to each complete number.
edgeCases: The root itself is a leaf.
Leading zero-valued nodes must not change place-value behavior.
Two leaves share a long prefix.
129.complexity: Target O(n) time and O(h) stack space using numeric prefixes. Rebuilding strings at each node adds length-dependent copying.

137.summary: Recover the value that appears once when every other integer appears three times.
137.approach: Count the set bits independently at each of the fixed-width bit positions. Every triplicated value contributes a multiple of three, so each count modulo three reconstructs the exceptional value; interpret the sign bit correctly.
edgeCases: The unique value is negative.
The unique value is zero.
Repeated negative values exercise sign handling.
137.complexity: O(nw) time and O(1) auxiliary space for fixed word width w, commonly 32; a bit-state machine reduces the scan to constant word operations per value.

142.summary: Find the node where a linked-list cycle begins, or determine that no cycle exists.
142.approach: First use slow and fast pointers to find a meeting point inside a cycle. Then reset one pointer to the head and move both one step at a time; their next meeting is the cycle entry because the initial path lengths differ by whole cycle lengths.
edgeCases: The list is acyclic.
The tail links directly to the head.
A one-node list points to itself.
142.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space; compare node identity, not node values.

148.summary: Sort a linked list by rearranging its node links.
148.approach: Apply merge sort: split the list into two halves, sort both, and merge them by relinking the smaller head each time. A bottom-up version merges runs of doubling lengths to remove recursive stack usage.
edgeCases: An empty or singleton list is already sorted.
Many nodes have the same value.
A descending list requires changes throughout.
148.complexity: O(n log n) time. Top-down merge sort uses O(log n) recursion; iterative bottom-up merging reaches O(1) extra space.

149.summary: Find the largest group of given points that lie on one straight line.
149.approach: Choose each point as an anchor and count the other points by normalized direction. Reduce integer coordinate differences by their greatest common divisor and normalize the sign so equivalent slopes share a key without floating-point rounding.
edgeCases: All points lie on a vertical line.
Horizontal and diagonal lines tie in size.
Negative coordinate differences represent the same slope.
149.complexity: O(n²) direction comparisons and O(n) map space; exact normalization adds a gcd cost dependent on coordinate magnitude.

151.summary: Reverse the order of words in a string while normalizing separators to single spaces.
151.approach: Scan or split the input into nonempty words, ignoring leading, trailing, and repeated spaces. Reverse the word sequence and join it once, keeping the letters inside each word in their original order.
edgeCases: The input has leading and trailing spaces.
Several spaces occur between words.
There is only one word.
151.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output/intermediate storage for immutable strings; an editable character buffer permits an in-place variant.

160.summary: Find the shared node at which two acyclic linked lists merge, if one exists.
160.approach: Advance two pointers, switching each to the other list’s head after it reaches the end. Each pointer then traverses the same combined distance, aligning them at the common suffix or at null when the lists are disjoint.
edgeCases: The two heads already reference the same node.
Lists contain equal values but share no nodes.
The lists have very different lengths.
