160.complexity: O(m + n) time and O(1) extra space; the argument assumes acyclic lists and node-identity comparisons.

162.summary: Locate any array position that is larger than its neighbors, treating positions outside the array as lower than every value.
162.approach: Compare the middle value with its right neighbor. If the slope rises, a peak exists to the right; otherwise a peak exists in the remaining left range including the middle, so binary search can safely discard half the candidates.
edgeCases: A one-element array has a peak at index zero.
A strictly increasing array peaks at its end.
Several peaks are acceptable answers.
162.complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) extra space, using the problem’s unequal-adjacent-values assumption.

172.summary: Count the zeros at the end of n factorial without computing the factorial itself.
172.approach: Each trailing zero needs a factor pair of two and five, and factors of five are scarcer. Add the counts of multiples of 5, 25, 125, and so on, since higher powers contribute additional fives.
edgeCases: n below 5 contributes no zeros.
n = 25 includes an extra contribution from 25.
n = 0 uses 0! = 1.
172.complexity: O(log5 n) time and O(1) space; repeated integer division avoids overflow when generating powers of five.

173.summary: Expose a search tree’s values through an iterator that returns the next smallest value on demand.
173.approach: Keep the leftmost unvisited path on a stack. Pop one node for next, then push the leftmost path from its right child; the stack top always represents the next inorder value.
edgeCases: The tree contains only one node.
A left-heavy tree makes initialization deep.
hasNext becomes false immediately after the final value.
173.complexity: O(h) initialization and storage; next is O(h) worst-case but O(1) amortized over a full traversal, and hasNext is O(1).

188.summary: Maximize stock-trading profit with a configurable upper limit on completed transactions.
188.approach: Track the best cash and holding balances for each number of completed or available trades, using a clearly defined state convention. Update each day without accidentally reusing incompatible states; when k is at least half the number of days, use the unlimited-transactions simplification.
edgeCases: k = 1 reduces to a single buy-sell opportunity.
k exceeds the number of possible buy-sell pairs.
All prices decline.
188.complexity: O(nk) time and O(k) space with rolling states; the large-k shortcut takes O(n) time.

205.summary: Check whether one string can be relabeled character by character to produce another using a one-to-one mapping.
205.approach: Maintain mappings in both directions while reading corresponding positions. Reject a conflicting assignment in either map; checking only one direction would allow two distinct source characters to collapse onto the same target character.
edgeCases: Repeated source characters map to different targets.
Distinct source characters try to share one target.
A character is allowed to map to itself.
205.complexity: O(n) expected time and O(u) space for u distinct characters; fixed-size character alphabets bound the storage.

216.summary: Choose exactly k distinct digits from 1 through 9 whose total reaches a target.
216.approach: Backtrack in increasing digit order so each combination is generated once. Carry the remaining count and sum, and prune when the smallest or largest possible remaining digits cannot reach that sum.
edgeCases: The target is too small for k distinct digits.
k = 9 leaves only the full set as a candidate.
A sum is possible only by repeating a digit, which is forbidden.
216.complexity: O(2^9 × k) is a safe fixed-domain bound including result copies; recursion uses O(k), excluding output.

221.summary: Find the area of the largest all-one square inside a binary matrix.
221.approach: Let each DP value represent the largest square ending at that cell. A one-valued cell extends the minimum of its upper, left, and upper-left neighbors; a zero-valued cell resets the size to zero, and the largest side length is squared for the answer.
edgeCases: Every cell is zero.
The matrix has a single row or column.
One interior zero prevents a larger surrounding square.
221.complexity: O(rows × columns) time and O(columns) rolling-DP space; a full table or memoized version uses O(rows × columns).

222.summary: Count nodes in a complete binary tree faster than visiting every node.
222.approach: Compare the leftmost and rightmost heights of a subtree. Equal heights identify a perfect subtree with 2^h - 1 nodes; otherwise recurse into its children, exploiting completeness so most subtrees can be counted at once.
edgeCases: The tree is empty.
The tree is perfect.
Only the first slot of the final level is occupied.
222.complexity: O(log² n) time and O(log n) recursion on a complete tree; the shortcut is not valid for arbitrary tree shapes.

224.summary: Evaluate an arithmetic expression containing integers, addition, subtraction, parentheses, and spaces.
224.approach: Scan numbers while maintaining a running subtotal and the sign of the next term. On an opening parenthesis, save the outer subtotal and sign; on closing, combine the completed inner value with that saved context, allowing unary minus through the sign state.
edgeCases: The expression begins with a negative number.
A minus sign precedes a parenthesized expression.
Nested parentheses contain extra spaces.
224.complexity: O(n) time and O(depth) stack space; use an integer type wide enough for intermediate values.

228.summary: Summarize a sorted sequence of distinct integers as maximal consecutive ranges.
228.approach: Start a range at the current value and extend it while adjacent values differ by one. Emit a singleton or a start-to-end label only when a gap or the end of the input closes the range.
edgeCases: The input is empty.
Every value is isolated.
A range includes negative values and zero.
228.complexity: O(n) time plus formatting cost and O(1) auxiliary state, excluding output; avoid overflow in successor comparisons.

234.summary: Determine whether the values of a linked list form a palindrome.
234.approach: Find the midpoint with slow and fast pointers, then reverse one half. Compare matching nodes from the two halves, and reverse the modified half again if preserving the caller’s original list is part of the contract.
edgeCases: A singleton is palindromic.
An odd-length list has an unpaired center.
A mismatch appears only near the center.
234.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space with in-place reversal; restoring the list remains linear time.

236.summary: Find the lowest tree node whose subtree contains both target nodes in an arbitrary binary tree.
236.approach: Use postorder recursion that returns a found target or a subtree’s ancestor candidate. If both children return a match, the current node joins the two paths; if only one does, propagate it upward, treating a target node itself as a match.
edgeCases: One target is an ancestor of the other.
The targets lie in opposite root subtrees.
A skewed tree produces a deep search.
236.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) stack space. The usual early-return formulation assumes both target nodes exist, as in the official problem.

240.summary: Search a matrix whose rows and columns are each sorted, without assuming row ranges are disjoint.
240.approach: Start at the top-right corner. A value above the target eliminates its entire column, while a value below the target eliminates its entire row; each comparison removes a region that cannot contain the target.
edgeCases: The target is outside the matrix’s value range.
The matrix has only one row.
Repeated values appear across several rows and columns.
240.complexity: O(rows + columns) time and O(1) extra space with the corner walk.

274.summary: Compute the largest h for which at least h papers have at least h citations each.
274.approach: Bucket citation counts, placing every count above the number of papers into the final bucket. Accumulate papers from the largest bucket downward and return the first h whose accumulated count reaches h; sorting is a simpler alternative.
edgeCases: All papers have zero citations.
One paper has an extremely large citation count.
Exactly h papers have exactly h citations.
274.complexity: Bucket target: O(n) time and O(n) space. Sorting takes O(n log n), with auxiliary space depending on the sorting implementation.

283.summary: Move zero values to the end of an array while preserving the order of all other values.
283.approach: Maintain a write position for the next nonzero value and scan the array once. Compact nonzero values in order, then fill the remaining suffix with zeroes, or use swaps that preserve the same prefix invariant.
edgeCases: The array contains only zeroes.
No zeroes are present.
Zeroes alternate with repeated nonzero values.
283.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space; operate on the original array.

289.summary: Compute one simultaneous update of a cellular grid using each cell’s eight neighbors.
289.approach: Encode both the old and new state in each cell while making the first pass. Count neighbors using only the old-state bit, write the next-state bit from the birth and survival rules, then discard the old bit in a second pass.
edgeCases: An isolated live cell dies.
A dead cell with exactly three live neighbors is born.
Border cells have fewer than eight neighbors.
289.complexity: O(rows × columns) time and O(1) extra space with bit encoding; copying the board instead requires O(rows × columns) space.

290.summary: Check whether words follow the same one-to-one repetition pattern as a sequence of symbols.
290.approach: First ensure the number of words matches the number of pattern symbols. Maintain symbol-to-word and word-to-symbol maps, rejecting any contradiction so the mapping remains a bijection.
edgeCases: The word count differs from the pattern length.
Two different symbols map to the same word.
A repeated symbol is paired with a new word.
290.complexity: O(total input characters) expected time and O(distinct words + symbols) map entries, plus token storage.

328.summary: Group linked-list nodes at odd positions before nodes at even positions, preserving order within each group.
328.approach: Keep separate tails for the odd and even positional chains, retaining the original even head. Alternate link updates until the even chain ends, then connect the odd tail to the saved even head; positions, not values, determine the groups.
edgeCases: A two-node list keeps its order.
An odd-length list ends with an odd-positioned node.
Node values may all be equal.
328.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space with node reuse.

334.summary: Decide whether an array contains three strictly increasing values in increasing index order.
334.approach: Track the smallest first value and the smallest possible second value seen so far. Replace the first or second bound when a value improves it; a value above both bounds proves that an increasing triple has already formed.
edgeCases: Equal values do not form a strictly increasing triple.
The array is decreasing.
A new minimum arrives after a useful second bound.
334.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space; the two bounds summarize candidate subsequences, not necessarily one fixed pair.

345.summary: Reverse only the vowels of a string while leaving all other characters in their positions.
345.approach: Use two pointers that skip nonvowels from opposite ends of a mutable character buffer. Swap the vowels they find and move inward, recognizing both uppercase and lowercase vowel characters.
edgeCases: The string contains no vowels.
Uppercase and lowercase vowels are mixed.
Exactly one vowel needs no swap.
345.complexity: O(n) time; O(n) storage for an immutable-string result, or O(1) extra space if an editable buffer is supplied.

373.summary: Return up to k index pairs with the smallest sums from two sorted arrays.
373.approach: Treat each element of the first array as the start of a sorted stream of sums with the second array. Seed a min-heap with the first pair from up to k streams; after removing a pair, insert the next pair from that same stream.
edgeCases: k exceeds the total number of possible pairs.
Repeated values yield distinct index pairs with equal sums.
One array contains a single element.
373.complexity: For t = min(k, mn) and h = min(k, m), O(h + t log(h + 1)) time with heapify and O(h) auxiliary space, excluding output.

380.summary: Design a mutable set that supports membership changes and uniform random sampling efficiently.
380.approach: Store values in a dense array and map each value to its array index. To delete, move the final value into the removed slot and repair its index before popping; sampling a uniformly random array index then gives every current value equal probability.
edgeCases: Inserting an existing value must report failure.
Deleting the final array element needs careful index cleanup.
Sampling a singleton always returns that value.
380.complexity: Expected O(1) insert, delete, and random access with O(n) storage; dynamic-array growth is amortized and sampling assumes a nonempty set.

383.summary: Check whether available letter occurrences are sufficient to build a requested message.
383.approach: Count the available occurrences of each letter, then consume one for each requested letter. A count dropping below zero proves that some occurrence is missing; repeated letters must be counted rather than tracked only for presence.
edgeCases: A required letter never appears in the supply.
A letter appears in both strings but not often enough.
The supply contains unused extra letters.
383.complexity: O(m + n) time and O(1) counting space for the fixed lowercase alphabet; a general alphabet needs O(u) counters.

392.summary: Determine whether one string can be read in order from another while skipping arbitrary characters.
392.approach: Scan the longer string once and advance the shorter string’s pointer only on a match. Matching the earliest available occurrence never removes a better future choice, so reaching the end of the shorter string is sufficient.
edgeCases: The requested subsequence is empty.
The source string is empty but the request is not.
Required letters exist but appear in the wrong order.
392.complexity: O(n) scan time and O(1) space for a single query; many queries can justify indexing source-character positions.

433.summary: Find the fewest valid one-character mutations that transform a starting gene into a target gene.
433.approach: Model allowed genes as graph vertices and run breadth-first search from the start. Generate neighbors by trying each permitted letter at each position, accepting only unvisited genes in the bank; the first target reached has the fewest mutations.
edgeCases: The target is absent from the bank.
The bank contains genes that are unreachable from the start.
Several mutation routes have different lengths.
433.complexity: For B bank entries and length L, generating and hashing copied strings can cost O(BL²); with the official fixed gene length this is O(B). Storage is O(BL).

437.summary: Count downward tree paths with a specified sum, allowing paths to start and end below the root.
437.approach: During depth-first traversal, count prefix sums only along the current root-to-node path. For running sum s, every earlier prefix s-target defines a valid ending path; increment before descending and decrement on return so sibling branches do not contaminate each other.
edgeCases: Zero-valued nodes create several overlapping valid paths.
Negative values invalidate simple sum-threshold pruning.
A path can begin at an internal node.
437.complexity: O(n) expected time and O(h) path-map and stack space; worst-case height is n.

438.summary: List every position where a fixed-length window is an anagram of a supplied pattern.
438.approach: Build the pattern’s character counts and maintain the same counts for a sliding window of equal length. Remove the outgoing character and add the incoming one, recording a start whenever the frequency vectors agree.
edgeCases: The pattern is longer than the search string.
Valid windows overlap.
The pattern contains repeated letters.
438.complexity: O(n + m) time with fixed-size alphabet comparisons and O(1) counting space, excluding output; a general alphabet comparison adds an alphabet-size factor.

443.summary: Compress consecutive character runs into a mutable buffer using a character followed by its count when needed.
443.approach: Read one complete run at a time and write its character at the next output position. For runs longer than one, write each decimal count digit separately; the write position never overtakes unread input because the encoding cannot expand a run.
edgeCases: A run of one omits the count.
A run longer than nine produces multiple count digits.
Separated runs of the same character stay separate.
443.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space if count digits are emitted arithmetically; converting a count to text uses O(log n) temporary characters. Only the returned-length prefix matters.

452.summary: Choose the fewest point positions that intersect every closed interval representing a balloon.
452.approach: Sort intervals by their right endpoint and place an arrow at the earliest ending interval’s endpoint. Reuse that arrow for each interval containing it; once an interval begins beyond the arrow, start a new group with an arrow at its endpoint.
edgeCases: Two intervals touch at one endpoint and share an arrow.
All intervals overlap.
Every interval is disjoint from the others.
452.complexity: O(n log n) time for sorting and O(1) greedy state; sorting may require additional implementation-dependent workspace.

530.summary: Find the smallest value difference between any two nodes of a binary search tree.
530.approach: Traverse the search tree in inorder so values arrive sorted. Compare each value only with its immediate predecessor, because a nonadjacent pair cannot beat all differences between neighboring values.
edgeCases: The closest values lie in different subtrees.
The tree is a long chain.
The smallest gap occurs near one endpoint of the sorted order.
530.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) traversal stack space; the official problem provides at least two nodes.

547.summary: Count connected groups of cities described by a symmetric adjacency matrix.
547.approach: For each unvisited city, launch a graph traversal and count one new component. Mark all cities reachable from that start before moving on, so every component contributes exactly once even when it contains cycles.
edgeCases: Every city is isolated except for its diagonal entry.
All cities are mutually connected.
Two dense groups have no connecting edge.
547.complexity: O(n²) time to scan the matrix and O(n) visited/traversal space, excluding the input matrix.

605.summary: Determine whether enough flowers can be added to a row without placing adjacent flowers.
605.approach: Scan left to right and plant at the earliest empty position whose neighbors are also empty or outside the row. Taking that earliest feasible position does not reduce the room available farther right; update the effective previous state before continuing.
edgeCases: The requested number of new flowers is zero.
A single empty position can hold one flower.
Existing flowers constrain both ends of an empty run.
605.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra state; an implementation that writes planted flowers mutates the input.

637.summary: Compute the mean node value separately for every depth of a binary tree.
637.approach: Use breadth-first traversal with a fixed count of nodes for the current level. Accumulate that level’s sum before dividing by its count, and enqueue children for the next iteration.
edgeCases: A single-node tree has one average.
A level contains large values that can overflow a narrow integer sum.
Uneven branches still contribute to their actual depths.
637.complexity: O(n) time and O(width) queue space, excluding output; use a real queue or head index rather than repeated array shifts.

643.summary: Find the largest average among all contiguous subarrays of a fixed length.
643.approach: Compute the sum of the first complete window, then slide it by subtracting the outgoing value and adding the incoming value. Compare sums throughout and divide the best sum by the fixed length only once.
edgeCases: All values are negative.
The window length equals the array length.
The best window appears at the final possible start.
643.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space; initialize from an actual window rather than assuming the maximum starts at zero.

700.summary: Find a target value in a binary search tree and return the subtree rooted at its node.
700.approach: Compare the target with the current node and follow only the side that can contain it. Stop at an exact match or a missing child; the search-tree ordering makes exploring the other branch unnecessary.
edgeCases: The target is the root value.
The target is absent.
A skewed tree behaves like a linked list.
700.complexity: O(h) time, ranging from O(log n) when balanced to O(n) when skewed; O(1) extra space for an iterative search.

714.summary: Maximize trading profit when each completed transaction pays a fixed fee and at most one share is held.
714.approach: Maintain the best cash balance with no share and the best balance while holding one. Update from the previous day’s states, charging the fee consistently at either purchase or sale; allowing a state to stay unchanged represents skipping the day.
edgeCases: The fee exceeds every possible price gain.
Several small rises are better combined into one trade.
Prices remain constant.
714.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) state; charge the fee once per transaction, not at both buy and sell.

724.summary: Find the earliest index whose elements to the left and right have equal sums.
724.approach: Compute the total sum and maintain a running left sum. At each index, derive the right sum by subtracting the left sum and current value from the total, checking equality before adding the current value to the left side.
edgeCases: Index zero can be the answer with an empty left side.
Negative values can create several valid pivots.
No index balances the sums.
724.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space; return the first matching index during the forward scan.

790.summary: Count tilings of a two-row board using dominoes and L-shaped trominoes, modulo the required modulus.
790.approach: Use DP states for fully filled prefixes and prefixes with one corner gap; gap states capture the ways trominoes cross a boundary. Eliminating the gap states yields f(n) = 2f(n-1) + f(n-3), starting from f(0)=1, f(1)=1, and f(2)=2.
edgeCases: Width one has a single vertical-domino tiling.
Width two establishes the two base tilings.
Large widths require reducing intermediate counts modulo the specified modulus.
790.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) rolling-state space for the recurrence; count arithmetic must preserve exact modular values.

841.summary: Decide whether keys discovered while visiting rooms allow access to every room from the initial room.
841.approach: Treat room keys as directed edges and traverse from room zero. Mark a room when it is first discovered, then visit each newly reachable room once; success means the visited count equals the number of rooms.
edgeCases: A room contains a key to itself.
Keys form a cycle that omits another room.
The last room is reachable only through a long chain.
841.complexity: O(rooms + keys) time and O(rooms) visited/traversal space.

872.summary: Compare two trees by the left-to-right sequence of values at their leaves.
872.approach: Traverse each tree in left-before-right order and emit values only for leaves. Compare the resulting sequences, or compare two lazy leaf iterators to stop at the first difference without collecting every leaf.
edgeCases: The trees have different shapes but identical leaf sequences.
The same leaf values occur in a different order.
One tree has fewer leaves than the other.
872.complexity: O(n + m) time. Collecting leaves takes O(leaves + heights) space; paired lazy DFS iterators need O(h1 + h2).

909.summary: Find the minimum die rolls needed to reach the last square on a board with snakes and ladders.
909.approach: Run BFS over numbered squares, generating up to six next landing positions per state. Convert each number to the board’s alternating row coordinates and apply at most one snake or ladder for that roll before marking the destination visited.
edgeCases: A ladder immediately reaches the destination.
A snake returns to an already explored square.
Alternating row directions change the coordinate mapping.
909.complexity: O(N²) time and space for an N-by-N board, since each square has at most six candidate moves.

933.summary: Maintain a count of calls within a trailing time window as timestamps arrive in increasing order.
933.approach: Append each new timestamp to a queue, then remove timestamps strictly older than t-3000. The remaining queue represents the inclusive interval ending at the current call; monotone arrival times guarantee expired calls never become relevant again.
edgeCases: A call exactly 3000 units old still counts.
A long gap expires every earlier call.
Many closely spaced calls remain in the window.
933.complexity: O(1) amortized work per call with a queue and O(window population) storage; repeated array shifts can violate the time target.

1004.summary: Find the longest binary-array window that can become all ones by changing at most k zeroes.
1004.approach: Expand a sliding window while counting its zeroes. Whenever the count exceeds k, advance the left boundary until the budget is restored; record the length only for a window satisfying the zero budget.
edgeCases: k = 0 allows no zeroes in the window.
The array contains only zeroes.
k is large enough to cover every zero.
1004.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space because each pointer moves forward at most n times.

1161.summary: Find the earliest tree level whose node values have the maximum sum.
1161.approach: Traverse one level at a time with BFS and total its values. Update the winning level only when its sum is strictly larger than the best so far, preserving the smaller level number when sums tie.
edgeCases: All level sums are negative.
Two levels tie for the maximum.
The root alone is the winning level.
1161.complexity: O(n) time and O(width) queue space, excluding the input tree.

1207.summary: Check whether each distinct array value has a different occurrence count.
1207.approach: Count occurrences in a map, then insert those counts into a set. A repeated count means two different values occur equally often, while matching map and set sizes establishes uniqueness.
edgeCases: Every array value is identical.
Two distinct values each occur once.
Negative and positive values have matching frequencies.
1207.complexity: O(n) expected time and O(u) space for u distinct values.

1268.summary: Return up to three lexicographically earliest product suggestions after each additional search character.
1268.approach: Sort the products and keep the range still matching the current prefix. Shrink its left and right boundaries when their next character fails to match, then take its first three products; the surviving range only narrows as the prefix grows.
edgeCases: The first search character matches no product.
A product ends before a later search character.
More than three products share a prefix.
1268.complexity: With N products, maximum product length L, and query length M: sorting costs O(N log N × L) character work; range narrowing is O(N + M), plus O(M) result references. Sorting workspace varies.

1318.summary: Count the fewest bit changes needed so the bitwise OR of two integers equals a target.
1318.approach: Inspect each bit position independently. A target zero requires clearing every contributing one in both inputs, while a target one requires one flip only if both input bits are zero; sum these independent costs.
edgeCases: The current OR already equals the target.
Both inputs have a one where the target has zero, requiring two flips.
Both inputs have zero where the target has one.
1318.complexity: O(w) time and O(1) space for word width w; JavaScript bitwise operations use signed 32-bit values, so wider domains need different handling.

1372.summary: Find the longest downward tree path whose edge directions alternate between left and right.
1372.approach: At each node, track the lengths of alternating paths that could continue through a left edge and a right edge. A continuation uses the child’s opposite-direction state, while a fresh path can start at every node; measure lengths in edges.
edgeCases: A single-node tree has path length zero.
A straight one-direction chain cannot keep alternating.
The best path starts below the root.
1372.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) DFS stack space; returning two lengths per node is sufficient.

1431.summary: For each child, check whether giving that child all extra candies would reach the current largest candy count.
1431.approach: Find the maximum existing count once. Compare each child’s count plus the extra amount with that maximum, treating ties as successful; each comparison describes a separate hypothetical allocation.
edgeCases: Several children already share the maximum.
Enough extra candies can make every child a possible maximum.
A smaller count becomes exactly equal to the maximum.
1431.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the n boolean results.

1456.summary: Find the largest number of vowels within a substring of a specified length.
1456.approach: Count vowels in a fixed-size sliding window using a constant-size vowel set. Add the entering character’s contribution and remove the leaving character’s contribution, retaining the largest count among complete windows.
edgeCases: The window length equals one.
The input contains no vowels.
A complete window contains only vowels.
1456.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space; a count of k is an immediate global upper bound.

1466.summary: Count road reversals needed so every city can follow directed roads to city zero in an underlying tree.
1466.approach: Build an undirected traversal graph while retaining each road’s original direction. Traverse outward from city zero and count every discovered edge pointing away from the root; each such edge must reverse because the underlying tree gives no alternate route.
edgeCases: All roads already point toward city zero.
Every road along a chain points away from zero.
A star around zero mixes inward and outward directions.
1466.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) adjacency/visited space for n cities; the argument relies on the underlying graph being a tree.

1493.summary: Find the longest run of ones achievable after deleting exactly one element from a binary array.
1493.approach: Maintain a sliding window containing at most one zero. Its usable length is window length minus one, which accounts for deleting the zero or, in an all-one window, deleting a one as the problem still requires.
edgeCases: An all-one array returns its length minus one.
A single-element array becomes empty.
Two zeroes force the left boundary to move.
1493.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space; exactly one deletion distinguishes this from an at-most-one-flip problem.

1657.summary: Decide whether two strings can be transformed into one another through position swaps and global exchanges of existing character labels.
1657.approach: Compare both the set of characters present and the multiset of their frequencies. Position swaps remove ordering constraints, and global label exchanges can permute frequency assignments, but cannot introduce a character that was absent.
edgeCases: The strings have different lengths.
Frequency multisets match but character sets differ.
The same character set has incompatible frequency counts.
1657.complexity: O(n + alphabet log alphabet) time and O(alphabet) space; for a fixed 26-letter alphabet this is O(n) time and O(1) space.

1679.summary: Form as many disjoint pairs as possible whose values sum to a target.
1679.approach: Keep frequencies of values waiting for partners. For each new value, consume one available complement if possible; otherwise store the value, ensuring every occurrence participates in at most one pair.
edgeCases: The target is twice a repeated value.
An odd number of identical values leaves one unused.
No pair reaches the target.
1679.complexity: O(n) expected time and O(u) frequency storage; sorting and two pointers offer O(n log n) time with sorting-dependent space.

1732.summary: Compute the highest altitude reached from a sequence of signed changes, starting at altitude zero.
1732.approach: Accumulate changes into the current altitude and update a running maximum after each step. Initialize the maximum to zero so the starting point remains a candidate even when every later point is lower.
edgeCases: Every change is negative.
The route reaches its maximum on the last step.
A rise returns only to the starting altitude.
1732.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

1926.summary: Find the fewest steps from a maze entrance to a different open boundary cell.
1926.approach: Run BFS through open cells, marking them when enqueued to avoid duplicate work. The first reached boundary cell other than the entrance is the nearest exit because BFS explores in nondecreasing distance.
edgeCases: The entrance itself lies on the boundary but does not count as an exit.
Walls isolate the entrance.
Several exits exist at different distances.
1926.complexity: O(rows × columns) time and space; marking the grid saves a separate visited array but mutates the input.

2095.summary: Remove the middle node of a linked list, choosing the later middle when its length is even.
2095.approach: Advance a slow pointer one step and a fast pointer two steps, retaining the predecessor of the slow pointer. When the fast pointer reaches the end, bypass the slow node; handle the singleton separately because it has no predecessor.
edgeCases: A singleton becomes an empty list.
A two-node list loses its second node.
An odd-length list loses its unique central node.
2095.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space through a single midpoint traversal.

2130.summary: Find the largest sum of nodes paired symmetrically from opposite ends of an even-length linked list.
2130.approach: Locate the midpoint and reverse one half so corresponding twin nodes can be traversed together. Compute each pair sum once, retaining the maximum, and restore the reversed half if the caller requires the list to remain unchanged.
edgeCases: A two-node list has one twin pair.
The maximum pair is nearest the middle.
Equal-valued nodes give several equal maxima.
2130.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space with in-place reversal; a copied-value array uses O(n) space instead.

2215.summary: Return the distinct values present in each of two arrays but absent from the other.
2215.approach: Convert both arrays into sets to remove duplicate occurrences. Build one result from values in the first set but not the second, and the other from the reverse difference.
edgeCases: Both arrays contain the same distinct values.
Repeated occurrences must appear only once in a result.
The two sets are disjoint.
2215.complexity: O(m + n) expected time and O(m + n) space including the sets and output.

2300.summary: For each spell strength, count potion strengths whose product reaches a success threshold.
2300.approach: Sort the potions, then binary-search the first successful potion for each positive spell. Every later potion also succeeds, so the answer is the suffix length; integer ceiling division can express the threshold without an overflowing product.
edgeCases: A product exactly equal to the threshold succeeds.
A spell works with no potion.
Repeated potion strengths all contribute separately.
2300.complexity: O(p log p + s log p) time for p potions and s spells, plus sorting workspace and O(s) output; ensure products or threshold calculations remain exact.

2336.summary: Represent an initially infinite positive-integer set supporting removal of its smallest value and restoration of removed values.
2336.approach: Keep a frontier for the smallest never-removed integer and a min-heap for smaller values that were added back. A companion membership set prevents duplicate heap entries; pop from the heap when possible, otherwise return and advance the frontier.
edgeCases: Adding back a value that is already present changes nothing.
The same removed value is added back repeatedly.
A restored small value precedes the untouched frontier.
2336.complexity: With b restored values buffered, heap operations take O(log(b + 1)), while a frontier pop takes O(1); storage is O(b), not proportional to an infinite range.

2352.summary: Count row-column pairs whose full sequences of matrix values are identical.
2352.approach: Use each row’s entire ordered sequence as a frequency-map key. Construct each column sequence and add the matching row frequency, so duplicate rows contribute the correct multiplicity rather than a single match.
edgeCases: Several identical rows match one column.
A one-cell matrix has one matching pair.
Ambiguous string concatenation must not confuse sequences like [1,23] and [12,3].
2352.complexity: O(n²) time and O(n²) key storage for an n-by-n matrix with collision-safe sequence keys; naive pairwise comparison costs O(n³).

2390.summary: Process deletions in a character stream where each star removes the closest surviving character to its left.
2390.approach: Keep surviving characters on a stack. Push ordinary characters and pop for each star, then join the survivors once; the stack directly represents the current string after every processed prefix.
edgeCases: Successive stars remove successive earlier characters.
Every ordinary character is eventually removed.
An input with no stars stays unchanged.
2390.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) stack/output space. The official input guarantees each deletion is valid; defensive generalizations must define invalid-star behavior.

2462.summary: Hire k workers by repeatedly choosing the lowest-cost eligible worker from the first or last candidate windows of the remaining list.
2462.approach: Maintain disjoint left and right frontiers and a heap of eligible workers keyed by cost then original index. After removing a worker, refill from that same side if an unseen worker remains, taking care not to insert the overlapping middle region twice.
edgeCases: The two candidate windows overlap from the beginning.
Equal costs are resolved by the smaller original index.
k includes every worker.
2462.complexity: Let h = min(n, 2c) for candidate-window size c: O(h + k log(h + 1)) time with heapify and O(h) space; repeated sorting of candidates is slower.

2542.summary: Choose k shared indices to maximize a first-array sum multiplied by the smallest chosen second-array value.
2542.approach: Sort paired values by the second array in descending order and retain the best k-1 earlier first-array values in a min-heap. Add the current value, evaluate its second value times the sum when k items are present, then discard the smallest first-array value for the next iteration; each evaluation explicitly includes the current minimum.
edgeCases: k = 1 reduces the choice to individual paired products.
k equals the full array length.
Equal second-array values can arrive in any order.
2542.complexity: O(n log n + n log k) time and O(n + k) storage for paired sorting and the heap; use a numeric type that preserves the largest score exactly.
